Christmas in July? Why Stop There?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why do we let something like the calendar dictate our holidays?
  • Instead of condensing so much effort and so much merriment into such a ludicrously small window at the very end of the year with nothing but the bland hell of winter ahead of us, let’s maximize our time by stretching it out.
  • In a recent development, if the holiday season has wrapped by February 14, the weeks following are the shoulder season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why do we let something like the calendar dictate our holidays? The fact that Thanksgiving and Christmas are just four weeks apart means by the time you’ve returned from November family visits, unpacked, shopped, decorated, done the party circuit, bought gifts, and maybe—maybe—worked for a few days, you have to turn around and celebrate again. It’s exhausting and expensive and too warp-speed to feel like that much of a good time. I’m not arguing to ban Christmas—which I am using as a catchall for nondenominational winter holidays, however that looks to you—what I am proposing is, in fact, much more exciting. I think we should switch the dates of Christmas and Valentine’s Day.

Sources indicate that consider it! Instead of condensing so much effort and so much merriment into such a ludicrously small window at the very end of the year with nothing but the bland hell of winter ahead of us, let’s maximize our time by stretching it out. Valentine’s Day is for romance, whether that means watching Bridget Jones’s Diary with friends, eating overpriced meals at candlelit restaurants, making cards, or mainlining chocolates. So on December 24, celebrate platonic love with friends—à la Galentine’s Day, except we should think of a better name—and maybe go on a date on the 25th. If that date goes well: bam! You now have a plus-one to a Upcoming Year’s Eve party and a midnight make out partner.

In a recent development, if the holiday season has wrapped by February 14, the weeks following are the shoulder season. Life is slow. But by the time everyone trickles back home from watching Die Hard in their pajamas or shopping post-Christmas sales or going to the gym, you only have to survive one month until the sweet relief of spring in late March. Nothing makes more sense for how to survive the long nights and cold of winter.

So we go all-in on spring. Mid-April is when it likely won’t snow again; around then you no longer need heat—at least in Fresh York City—so let’s make that a national holiday celebrating warm weather with seasonal bouquets (tulips, lilacs, peonies), foraged ramps, and maybe specials on dry-cleaning winter coats or sales on shearling boots.

But why stop there? We in America could take a page from France, where May can have four(!) public holidays as a kind of summer practice run. I’d be more than happy to celebrate VE Day in solidarity: Liberté, égalité, holiday! In our version, maybe botanical gardens will be free to the public for picnics. Maybe amusement parks will be gratis? Maybe lobster rolls and strawberry shortcake will be handed out on the street? Can the first summer blockbuster of May be an annual event with free popcorn? This month of long weekends will culminate in Memorial Day barbecues, which is a perfect bookend to summer with Labor Day—no notes.

Let’s keep summer luxurious, so summer Fridays will not be at the discretion of employers but mandated by the government for those three months. The Fourth of July can stay where it is with the caveat that if it rains, we get to observe it on the next day forecast for hot dog weather. Nothing important happens in August—phone it in, federal holiday or not. Labor Day stays, of course. The week following it in Upcoming York is Fashion Week, which runs concurrently with the US Open for tennis—very busy but very social. We’re going to adopt that nationwide as a festive season soft launching the country into fall.

And finally, let’s turn our attention to that somber stretch of time between early September and Thanksgiving. We don’t get enough time off, so we will move Presidents’ Day from February to mid-October for another much-needed holiday. Then cook a big turkey dinner on Thanksgiving, see your extended family, watch football, whatever, and delight in the fact that you don’t have to do it again until February. But start figuring out your Valentine’s Day dates now—those prix fixe dinners with chocolate lava cakes really book up fast these days.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's key to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

According to recent reports, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that organization or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, enhancement the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nicolas Cage was more of a curiosity than a star in the early 1990s when he snagged the leading role in John Dahl's neo-Western/Noir "Red Rock West." He was squarely on the radar thanks to his standout performances in "Moonstruck" and "Raising Arizona" (not to mention, a coveted weirdo on the strength of his dynamic portrayal of Sailor Ripley in "Wild at Heart"). But could he singlehandedly sell a movie? Not yet.

Recent findings suggest that propaganda Films made "Wild at Heart," and the company's late co-founder, Steve Golin, shepherded some of the greatest filmmakers of our era from music videos/commercials to feature films. It wasn't always a smooth transition. Propaganda co-founder David Fincher, now considered one of our greatest living directors, got chewed up by the 20th Century Fox machinery while making "Alien 3." Meanwhile, music video veteran Antoine Fuqua delivered an aimlessly stylish dud in 1998 with "The Replacement Killers.".

It has been revealed that stumbles aside, Hollywood prized Propaganda's director roster for its technical proficiency. Studios wanted a brand fresh wave of stylists who'd studied the work of Ridley Scott, Tony Scott, and Alan Parker. And Cage, the abundantly talented actor nephew of Francis Ford Coppola, seemed like an off-kilter star at a time when grunge rock and offbeat entertainment like "Twin Peaks" was catching fire. So, Dahl doubled down on the vibe of the moment, cast Lara Flynn Boyle (Donna from "Twin Peaks"), threw counterculture legend Dennis Hopper in as a villain, and had the makings of a sleeper hit.

Alas, like Dahl's subsequent noir thriller "The Last Seduction" (one of the finest of its kind), "Red Rock West" was shunted to home entertainment, which killed its Oscar eligibility and made it look like a misfire in spite of its sparkling critical response. It was anything but, and now, you've the chance to discover it.

Industry observers note that "Red Rock West" stars Nicolas Cage as a Marine veteran who, having been bounced from legitimate oil-drilling work, winds up in the seedy, noir-ish kind of rural town where good work is available ... if you're willing to kill someone's spouse for a nifty life-insurance payoff. Sometimes, you just want to watch a mean-spirited neo-noir, and John Dahl brings the nastiness with dastardly elan. In this case, Cage's Michael Williams has been mistaken for "Lyle from Dallas," who's been hired by Kevin McCord (J.T. Walsh) to off Lara Flynn Boyle's Suzanne Brown. Lyle eventually arrives in town in the malevolent form of Dennis Hopper, and that's where the noir bedlam kicks into high gear.

It has been revealed that whereas most of the Propaganda Films directors were supreme stylists, Dahl was a classicist. "Red Rock West" and "The Last Seduction" were lean-and-mean thrillers — taut, sere, and brutally sexy. Dahl didn't traffic in the sweaty, sexual histrionics of "The Massive Sleep," "Purple Noon," and "After Dark, My Sweet." Physical intimacy is purely transactional in his noirs. This might be why "Red Rock West" was relegated to home entertainment as a high-toned Skinemax film. It's the slowest of burns. It's like the Coen Brothers' "Blood Simple" without the flashy craft and cheeky sense of humor. Just know that this gem of a movie is out there, and it's so very worth your while.

GTA 6's cheats are deeply hidden, and will require you to jump through a few hoops to start using them.

Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.

According to recent reports, [Ed. note: We're still working to hunt down every cheat code, but until we find them all, this will give you an idea of what you'll need to do to unlock them all.].

Update (Nov. 21): We've updated this guide with inputs for three cheat codes.

Industry observers note that if you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a newly introduced Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

According to recent reports, you won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a newly introduced Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

Sources indicate that notably, your progress throughout the game, even before beating it, does contribute to these requirements. By the time you roll credits and unlock the Cheats menu, you'll likely already have a few of them unlocked.

To activate a cheat code, first pull out your phone by pressing Up on your D-Pad. Then hold down L1 and R1 on the home screen. (We have only been able to test the PS5 version of the game so far, but our assumption is that you'll need to hold LB and RB on Xbox Series X.) While holding those buttons, you'll have to enter the unlocked code with the D-Pad. Based on our testing, you won't be able to activate a code until you've actually beaten the game and unlocked the Cheats menu.

Note that activating a cheat code will disable saving for the rest of your play session. You also won't be able to earn achievements while cheats are on. Always remember to save before activating a cheat so you don't lose any progress.

Industry News: 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system.
  • While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system. Where the producer's role was once seen as paramount in getting a film made and even in achieving a certain artistic vision, a film's achievements are now often attributed to the isolated decisions of the all-key director.

While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships. Though plenty of movies have two directors, the sustained union of two filmmakers over many years and/or films is rarer, and it warrants a closer look at the best of those recurring or long-lasting alliances. While the idea of the director usually implies one voice making the final decisions for the myriad creative components of a finished film, these directing duos prove that continuing that sense of collaboration into the chief position on a film set can bear rewarding fruit.

Here are the best directing duos of all time, ranked.

Jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro spent years honing their singular aesthetic in short films before making their feature debut with "Delicatessen," a pitch-black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic apartment building where a butcher-landlord keeps his tenants fed by turning unsuspecting newcomers into meat. Jeunet and Caro's penchant for grotesque faces and sickly yellow lighting helped make the film a sensation, earning it four César Awards, including Best First Film and Best Original or Adapted Screenplay.

"The City of Lost Children" saw them double down on their peculiar sensibility: a fable set in a decaying port city, where a prematurely aging scientist steals children's dreams and a gentle circus strongman, played by Ron Perlman, searches for his kidnapped little brother. Its macabre, nightmarish storybook whimsy remains one of the most singular visions in French cinema — an underseen, visually stunning masterpiece.

Industry observers note that then the partnership abruptly ended. Jeunet was tapped to direct "Alien Resurrection", and his subsequent films, most famously the candy-colored "Amélie," have generally been warmer and more polished. Meanwhile, Caro's lone solo feature, the sci-fi film "Dante 01," never found the same audience. It makes for a fascinating what-if, as nobody has quite matched the blend of cruelty and tenderness the two cooked up together, and it's hard not to suspect that the grime and the heart needed each other.

John Musker and Ron Clements met at Disney while working on "The Fox and the Hound," and they went on to become one of the studio's most dependable directing teams during its biggest creative revival. They made their feature-directing debut alongside Burny Mattinson and David Michener on 1986's "The Great Mouse Detective," a Sherlock Holmes riff about a sleuthing rodent, before Clements pitched an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid." Working with songwriters Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, they delivered a film that won Oscars for its score and for "Under the Sea" and helped kick off the Disney Renaissance.

In a recent development, "Aladdin" followed in 1992. The now-iconic musical was the highest-grossing film of its year and the highest-grossing animated film to that point, earning two more Oscars for Menken's score and "A Whole New World." The duo kept working through shifting tastes, with "Hercules" in 1997 and the sci-fi swashbuckler "Treasure Planet" in 2002, which flopped but has since found its defenders. They returned to hand-drawn animation with "The Princess and the Frog" in 2009, then made their first fully computer-animated feature with "Moana," which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. It also spawned a widely criticized, remarkably premature live-action remake — part of a trend the pair described as "bemusing.".

The pair has since retired, closing out a partnership that lasted more than three decades. Their films were defined by the fundamentals of Disney magic: musical numbers that developed the plot and emotions, and humor that never smothered the pathos underneath. Few directors have made so many movies that feel so effortlessly designed for all audiences.

Before they set box-office records, Joe and Anthony Russo were comedy filmmakers from Cleveland. After their micro-budget debut, "Pieces", Steven Soderbergh and George Clooney produced their second feature, "Welcome to Collinwood." The brothers broke through on television, winning an Emmy for directing the pilot of "Arrested Development," then directing the pilot of "Community" and many beloved episodes after it.

That sitcom background is key to the work that followed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where their instincts for staging a dozen characters trading blows and punchlines helped define the quippy, ensemble-driven sensibility of their "Avengers" movies. However, that style has become a grievance among certain viewers who wish the films could escape their unrelenting sense of brand management. The brothers have cited François Truffaut and the French Upcoming Wave as major influences, but their biggest films operate within decidedly conventional blockbuster boundaries. Still, there's no denying the level of control needed to orchestrate some of the biggest hits of the 2010s.

It has been revealed that their post-Marvel streaming films, including "Cherry," "The Gray Man," and "The Electric State," have been considerably less successful creatively. But through their organization AGBO, they also produced the far more inventive "Everything Everywhere All at Once." With "Avengers: Doomsday" scheduled for December 2026, the brothers are once again tasked with herding Hollywood's biggest cast into something halfway coherent — a feat they've proven capable of, against all odds.

Recent findings suggest that justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead work on the principle that a tiny budget and a big idea can take you a long way. They broke out with "Resolution," which premiered at Tribeca in 2012, a lo-fi two-hander about a man who holes up in a remote cabin with his drug-addicted friend while something strange lurks beyond the walls. "Spring" followed in 2014, a Lovecraftian romance set on the Italian coast that fuses monster spectacle with the heart of a character drama. Benson typically writes and Moorhead handles cinematography, but the two co-direct and often appear on screen.

Industry observers note that that approach led to "The Endless," in which they play brothers returning to the cult they escaped. The film explicitly connects to "Resolution", establishing a shared cosmic-horror mythology. "Synchronic," their 2019 time-bending drug thriller with Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, contains looser connections to that world, while the pandemic-era "Something in the Dirt" finds them starring as neighbors chasing a supernatural mystery.

Marvel took notice. They directed episodes of "Moon Knight" and much of the second season of "Loki," then helped rework the first season of "Daredevil: Born Again" before returning for its second. You could have worse pairs acting as custodians for one of the entertainment industry's biggest brands. Even if their Marvel work lacks the more personal flourishes of their smaller projects, you can still feel their indie-horror sensibility breaking through.

In a recent development, daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert met at Emerson College and built their reputation on music videos, most famously DJ Snake and Lil Jon's "Turn Down for What", before making their feature debut with "Swiss Army Man," an emotionally vulnerable absurdist comedy about Paul Dano befriending a flatulent corpse played by Daniel Radcliffe. The movie's surprisingly tender treatment of shame, loneliness, and the weird stuff that makes us human earned the duo the U.S. Dramatic Directing Award at Sundance in 2016.

According to recent reports, that set the stage for their true breakout: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" cranked their style to maximalist levels in one of the decade's most unexpected hits. Michelle Yeoh's exhausted laundromat owner is dragged across the multiverse in a hyper-stylized, daffy yet sincere family drama about an immigrant mother and her daughter facing the potential end of the world. It was A24's highest-grossing release at the time — the studio's first film to reach $100 million worldwide — and won seven of its 11 Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay, plus acting wins for Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Jamie Lee Curtis.

Sources indicate that that made the Daniels only the third directing pair to win Best Director, after Robert Wise & Jerome Robbins and Joel & Ethan Coen. Though prone to hyperactivity, few other filmmakers could make a hot-dog-fingers gag and a mother-daughter reconciliation feel like parts of the same carefully calculated thematic throughline. Here's hoping their next film, with Matt Damon attached, sustains that momentum.

Phil Lord and Christopher Miller have built a career on finding inventiveness in projects that might have become franchise mediocrity under other filmmakers. The Dartmouth classmates started in television, co-creating the short-lived MTV cult satire "Clone High," before making their feature debut with "Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs," a frantic, silly adaptation of a children's picture book filled with surprisingly clever gags and character detail.

In a recent development, the duo kept pace: "21 Jump Street," a seemingly ill-conceived reboot of a 1980s TV drama as a buddy-cop farce, became one of the 2010s' most successful and acclaimed comedies. "The LEGO Movie," seemingly a feature-length branding exercise, became an inventive parable about creativity and conformity, launching a franchise of other LEGO films while transforming a bad premise into a cinematic miracle.

Recent findings suggest that their commitment to a distinct filmmaking voice also caused friction within the franchise machine, leading to their firing from "Solo: A Star Wars Story" late in production, though they went on to find other successes. As producers of "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," they helped push the possibilities of mainstream animation forward. They also drew on their "Star Wars" experience in making 2026's "Project Hail Mary," a funny, meticulously crafted, heart-on-its-sleeve adaptation of Andy Weir's novel that has grossed roughly $685 million worldwide. The pair's irreverence remains central to their success: tongue-in-cheek self-awareness and a genuine love of subverting expectations have helped them turn unlikely premises into crowd-pleasers.

Sources indicate that lana and Lilly Wachowski came out of Chicago as comic-book obsessives, finding work as screenwriters before announcing themselves as directors with "Bound," a lean, sultry neo-noir starring Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon that demonstrated off their formal command on a small budget. Then came "The Matrix," the iconic 1999 sci-fi smash that fused Hong Kong martial arts, anime, and heady cyberpunk philosophy into a defining text of 2000s action cinema. Its "bullet time" effects were imitated endlessly; it broke box-office records, and cinema was never quite the same.

According to recent reports, but what really sets the sisters apart is how stubbornly they kept betting massive. "Speed Racer" may have flopped on release, but it has since gained recognition as a forward-thinking work of art. Similarly, "Cloud Atlas" and "Sense8," their Netflix series about psychically linked strangers, have attracted devoted defenders of the Wachowskis' uncompromising vision. Even "Jupiter Ascending" has its champions. Their work has also invited a deeper reading of "The Matrix" as a trans allegory, something Lilly has discussed directly.

Industry observers note that the sisters have pursued separate projects in recent years. Lana directed 2021's caustically self-referential "The Matrix Resurrections" on her own, while Lilly has been developing "The Hunted," a mid-sized thriller with an all-transgender cast. Even while working apart, both continue to follow the amplified, philosophical sensibilities that made their collaborations so distinctive.

In a recent development, widely known as engineers of feature-length anxiety attacks, Josh and Benny Safdie were among the most exciting filmmakers working in Upcoming York before their broader breakthrough. They first drew attention with "Daddy Longlegs," a scrappy, semi-autobiographical portrait of a chaotic father that played Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2009. Then came "Heaven Knows What," a bruising drama about people struggling with heroin addiction, starring Arielle Holmes and drawn from her own experiences and writings. Their method of handheld close-ups, overlapping dialogue, and nonprofessionals cast alongside movie stars came together in "Good Time," in which Robert Pattinson plays a small-time crook losing control of one long night.

The apex was "Uncut Gems," in which Adam Sandler gave a career-defining performance as a gambling-addicted Diamond District jeweler hurtling through two hours of escalating bad decisions — a stress-riddled, darkly funny drama of street-level chaos and apprehension.

In a recent development, the brothers have since pursued separate directing careers, and differences in their sensibilities emerged in their solo work. Benny's "The Smashing Machine," with Dwayne Johnson as MMA fighter Mark Kerr, struggled commercially but revealed a quieter, more observant side of his filmmaking. Josh's "Marty Supreme," with Timothée Chalamet as a force of chaos, continued the streak of relentless havoc. Both films still carry the fingerprints of what the two built together: textured environments, tightly observed characters, and an acute sense of the worlds they inhabit. But the partnership that produced "Uncut Gems" remains one of the most electrifying of its era.

Industry observers note that few partnerships have been as productive or as generous to film history as Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. Although Powell generally handled on-set direction and Pressburger originated many of their stories, they famously shared writing, producing, and directing credit during their peak years as the Archers. Powell, an Englishman who learned his craft on British quota quickies, and Pressburger, a Hungarian screenwriter who fled Nazi Germany, first teamed up in 1939. Pressburger later won an Oscar for the original story of 1941's "49th Parallel," and in the early 1940s they formed their production company, the Archers, whose films opened with an arrow striking a target.

That led to one of the great runs in British cinema: the wartime satire "The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp," the pastoral "A Canterbury Tale," the romance "I Know Where I'm Going!," and "A Matter of Life and Death," a fantasy about a pilot who cheats death. "Black Narcissus" won Oscars for Jack Cardiff's cinematography and Alfred Junge's art direction, while "The Red Shoes" remains an utterly dazzling film about artistic obsession, with its nearly 17-minute ballet sequence nestled inside a classical yet fantastical melodrama.

Their main partnership ended after 1957's "Ill Met by Moonlight," though they collaborated again on smaller projects, including "They're a Weird Mob" and "The Boy Who Turned Yellow." Powell's solo thriller "Peeping Tom" was so reviled by British critics that it badly damaged his career, though it has since been rediscovered as a masterpiece, thanks in no small part to Martin Scorsese.

Recent findings suggest that joel and Ethan Coen have long worked like one filmmaker with two heads, though Directors Guild rules obscured that for two decades by crediting Joel as director and Ethan as producer. The two also shared editing duties under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes, a nonexistent editor who nonetheless earned Oscar nominations for "Fargo" and "No Country for Old Men." They finally received joint directing credit with 2004's "The Ladykillers." By then, the work had long spoken for itself: "Blood Simple" and "Raising Arizona" announced a pair of formalists with a wicked sense of humor, and "Barton Fink" swept Cannes in 1991.

Working frequently with cinematographer Roger Deakins, they moved between screwball comedy ("Raising Arizona," "Burn After Reading"), gangster pictures ("Miller's Crossing"), and Westerns ("True Grit") with unmatched formal and tonal precision. Few filmmakers could make movies as equally iconic as "The Massive Lebowski" and "No Country for Old Men," works at opposite ends of the tonal spectrum that still feel unmistakably of a piece with the brothers' sardonic, philosophical sensibility.

After 2018's "The Ballad of Buster Scruggs," the brothers pursued solo directing projects, with Joel making "The Tragedy of Macbeth" and Ethan making "Drive-Away Dolls" and "Honey Don't!" But in October 2026, while receiving the Lumière Prize in Lyon, they noted they planned to direct another film together. Joel's upcoming "Jack of Spades," which Ethan co-wrote and Netflix plans to release theatrically in fall 2027, is still a solo directing project, but their reunion comments suggest another collaboration may be ahead. Hopefully they'll add another movie to a remarkable joint filmography, which we've ranked in full.

As a certified personal trainer, I work with a wide range of clients who have lots of different fitness goals. But for my clients in their 60s and beyond, there’s usually one objective that drives their training: improving balance and stability.

I recently started working with a 60-year-old client who wanted to focus on just that. She noticed that she was a little more unsteady on her feet than she used to be, and had a few close calls with falling. After a thorough check-up with her doctor, we began our work together with the following routine.

These exercises aren’t just for seniors. It’s never too early to start thinking about your balance, so give them a try during your next workout. They’re appropriate for any fitness level and you won’t need any equipment to do them (but adding a dumbbell or two will always make things more challenging).

Check in with your doctor before trying any latest workout, especially if you have balance concerns.

These exercises aren’t hard, but doing them correctly is notable. Beginners should consider meeting with a personal trainer or physical therapist for feedback and guidance on form, and to get modifications if needed.

You’ll just need some room and an elevated platform, like a stair step, for this workout. Hang onto a chair or another stable surface for additional support if you need it.

Recent findings suggest that start by doing each exercise for one set of 10 reps. As your balance improves, you can add an additional set and increase your reps to 12. You can also use small dumbbells for the step-up to balance to ramp up the difficulty.

These exercises can be done on their own or as a warm-up for other activities.

According to recent reports, you may feel muscle fatigue when doing this workout, but you should never feel sharp pain. Stop the workout immediately and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

Here’s how to do the exercises:.

The exercises in this workout force you to find equilibrium when your center of gravity is maintained over a smaller surface area – either one foot for the standing marches, step up to balance, and side step to balance, or a narrow placement of two feet for the heel-to-toe walks.

Industry observers note that during these exercises, your deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques engage to stabilize and support your entire body. Your glutes and hip stabilizing muscles also work to keep the hips in a level position. The stronger these muscles are, the more conditioned they’ll be to keep you upright and sturdy during everyday movement.

Additionally, exercises like the step-up to balance strengthen key muscle groups in your lower body, like the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

  • Ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roger Ebert wasn't as effusive about Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings" films as many other critics. For reference, Ebert gave "Fellowship of the Ring" and "The Two Towers" three stars (out of four) and then "Return of the King" three and a half.

Recent findings suggest that "A true visualization of [J.R.R.] Tolkien's Middle-earth it is not," wrote Ebert of Jackson's "Fellowship," arguing it "adds up to more of a sword and sorcery epic" that loses the "innocence" of the books. Though, Ebert conceded in that review that "That 'Fellowship of the Ring' doesn't match my imaginary vision of Middle-earth is my problem, not yours.".

Ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R. Tolkien." However, he praised "Return of the King" as a strong conclusion which solidified the trilogy as "a work of bold ambition at a time of cinematic timidity," even if he felt the film and trilogy fell "a little shy of greatness.".

But you know what fantasy movie Ebert did love? 2007's "The Golden Compass," adapted from Philip Pullman's "His Dark Materials" novels. It's set in an alternate world where a piece of every person's soul exists in the form of an animal, called a dæmon. British orphan Lyra Belacqua (Dakota Blue Richards) embarks on a quest to rescue a friend and stumbles onto a much more cosmic struggle. Ebert gave it four stars, writing:.

Industry observers note that "'The Golden Compass' is a darker, deeper fantasy epic than the 'Rings' trilogy, 'The Chronicles of Narnia' or the 'Potter' films. It springs from the same British world of quasi-philosophical magic, but creates more complex villains and poses more intriguing questions.".

While most would disagree with Ebert's quality assessment, he's onto something, as "Golden Compass" invites "Lord of the Rings" comparisons.

"The Golden Compass" was produced by Latest Line Cinema, the same production tech giant behind "The Lord of the Rings," and it's clear the studio was hoping to repeat its previous success. "The Golden Compass" even features two vital "Rings" alums: Ian McKellen (Gandalf) as the voice of polar bear king Iorek Byrnison, and Christopher Lee (the corrupted wizard Saruman) as a leader of the Magisterium, the Church of Lyra's world. It was reported in 2007 both actors were cast at New Line's behest.

But quite the contrary, "The Golden Compass" under-performed ($372 million in theaters against a $180 million budget), and sequels were never made. "The Golden Compass" even contributed to the end of Latest Line as an independent studio, as it was folded into Warner Bros. in 2008. Not helping the movie's financials was a religious backlash. The Magisterium allegorically represents all authoritarian religions but especially the Catholic Church, and "The Golden Compass" was in turn condemned by the Vatican.

Industry observers note that "The Golden Compass" didn't win over fans of its source novel, either, due to abundant changes. The movie cuts out the book's entire ending, which directly sets up the sequel, "The Subtle Knife." But the attacks on religion? Those are taken right from the book. Philip Pullman is an atheist, and "His Dark Materials" is his rebuttal to the Christian-themed British fantasies of J.R.R. Tolkien and "Chronicles of Narnia" author C.S. Lewis, particularly the latter as both stories are about children traveling to different worlds. (Though Tolkien, for what it's worth, is said to have disliked "Narnia.").

Industry observers note that "I cordially dislike allegory," Tolkien once famously claimed, believing it robs readers the freedom to interpret a work. For decades, said readers have since read into the influence of Tolkien's Catholic faith on his Middle-earth stories.

In a recent development, sauron and his ring are a Luciferian conception of evil: A fallen angel who rules a fiery, molten realm and whose darkness spreads as temptation. J. R. R. Tolkien's villain is the Devil, Philip Pullman's is the Church.

In a recent development, frodo carrying the ring echoes Christ carrying his own cross to Golgotha and, in turn, the metaphorical crosses that all of Christ's followers carry. "The Chronicles of Narnia," meanwhile, features talking lion Aslan as a direct allegory for the Christian God, Christ-like sacrifice and resurrection included.

Industry observers note that in "His Dark Materials," the Magisterium worships "the Authority," a name suggesting an "authority" is all that organized religion is. The Authority is also a liar: He is not the creator of the universe, merely the first "angel" who came into being. The weak and withered "god" eventually crumbles into dust, as if humanity has no more use for him. The very last dialogue of the trilogy is Lyra endeavoring to build a "Republic of Heaven" on Earth.

Yet, circling back to Roger Ebert, he disputed the anti-religious reading of the "Golden Compass" movie, arguing it reworks the Magisterium into a more purely political villain, "a Soviet dictatorship or Big Brother." He specifically praised the film's themes as "murky," compared to Pullman's blatant allegory for the death of God, and affirmed that "the controversy surrounding ['The Golden Compass'] obscures its function as a splendid entertainment.".

It has been revealed that amusingly, Ebert championed the movie for the same reasons many "His Dark Materials" fans rejected it. Toning down the anti-religion elements did not spare the movie the Church's wrath, either. One can only wonder what Ebert would have thought of the eventual "His Dark Materials" TV series that adapted Pullman's story to book fans' delight.

  • Today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era.
  • That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” indicates Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling the drawers out. I was fascinated with strings. It’s the closest instrument to the human voice. And I find it the most expressive instrument.”.

Today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era. By 14, Bell was performing with the Philadelphia Orchestra, and would soon be touring the world. “I live in hotels 250 days a year,” states Bell of the nonstop schedule he has maintained since his teens. Specifically, Bell has been “staying at the Langham for decades now,” he says, referring to the regal central London hotel that first opened in 1865. “I chose it on my own because it was near one of my favorite halls in London, which is the Wigmore Hall. And now I stay with them whenever I’m traveling.”.

That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.

Attendees included actor Simon Callow, House of Dragon actor Emily Carey, former British culture minister Ed Vaizey, Saturday Night Live UK cast producer Susie Hall, stage and television actor Indira Varma, and Verity actor Ismael Cruz Córdova.

Held in partnership with Vanity Fair, the evening marked the latest iteration of the Langham’s Luminaries in Residence program. The event series is continuation of the hotel’s legacy that brings together a diverse, influential community—an evocative reminder of prominent guests from its storied past, including Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, George Orwell, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain.

Industry observers note that “I’m not going to put my name in the same sentence as Toscanini or Mark Twain—who has stayed here, or Churchill, who has stayed here. But it’s cool to be part of the history,” states Bell. “So maybe someday, in a hundred years, there will be a violinist who might say that—that I stayed here. I don’t know, maybe that would mean something.”.

Sources indicate that it certainly does mean something. Pierce Brosnan and his wife, Keely Shaye Brosnan, “have been huge fans of Joshua for many, many years,” Brosnan tells me. “Keely went to go see him…I don’t know how many years back. Unfortunately, due to the LA traffic, she got there late, five minutes late, and they wouldn’t let her into the concert. So tonight is one of those nights.”.

Bell, who performed mid-dinner with members of the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields—with a surprise appearance from his wife, soprano Larisa Martínez—brought about a collective catharsis.

Recent findings suggest that dazzling, fiery, and flamboyant, the experience of watching Bell up close is impossible to replicate. “I just think he’s incredibly soulful, and there’s something really elegant,” actor Russell Tovey tells me, before explaining how he actually discovered Bell via his Instagram algorithm.

Sources indicate that for actor Lesley Manville, the event marked her introduction to Bell’s music. “I’m a bit embarrassed that he was not on my radar. But isn’t that nice to have a surprise like that?” claims Manville. “Schubert’s String Quintet is one of my favorite pieces of music. It’s unbelievably beautiful. You think of a violin, you think of those strings. And it’s instant emotion. They just make you cry.”.

There is a great power in being able to access the emotions of others, as Bell does.

According to recent reports, “I think it is the ultimate gift to be able to make people happy,” indicates Brosnan. “My job is being an entertainer—to take the words of great writing and try to transform it into something that is meaningful and memorable.”.

Speaking of entertaining, the week’s announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond was front of mind. “I wish him every joy and every success. He and I made a movie a number of years ago called Remember Me. I played his father. So I was very, very pleased and joyful for his nomination and now his success, and I believe he will be magnificent.”.

According to recent reports, and that creative full circle is exactly what the night was advocating. “Our own Luminaries in Residence program reflects our belief that meaningful hospitality creates genuine connection with extraordinary talents with one another, and with arts,” Bob van den Oord, CEO of Langham Hospitality Group, explained as he took the stage. “The Langham isn’t simply a place to stay, but a place to gather, exchange ideas, and indeed celebrate.”.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has a giant crab haunting the swamps and, more importantly, the Crabshack VF5 SMG, a crab-themed gun, to help your future career prospects. It's all part of an optional event called Pelican Valley Outpost that sees you pick up the pieces of some questionable experiments carried out on behalf of a store chain. It's worth the trouble, even aside from the standout weapon. There's some cash to help reach your next family fund milestone and a free jet ski, too. Best of all, this little excursion is completely safe, assuming you don't run afoul of the local gator population.

Below, we show you where to find the giant crab in GTA 6 so you can clear the Pelican Valley Outpost and get the Crabshack VF5 SMG.

Pelican Valley Outpost, where the giant crab research facility is, has several codes you need to find on your way to getting the standout weapon. You'll find it on a medium-sized island southwest of the "Pelican Valley" name label on the map. Once you remove the fog from the region map, you can see it's one of the only islands in the area with buildings on it.

In a recent development, take Jason's boat from his house, and set out. Definitely don't swim here, even if you're already nearby. There are too many gators for this to be a safe option. You can dock your boat at the boathouse and follow the jetty to the research facility proper. The boathouse is locked, but you'll get inside before leaving.

You'll see several buildings in the compound, but if you venture inside the first shack, you'll notice the power is off. You can still explore it, though you can't access the researcher's computer, which is essential for clearing the outpost. Head outside and around the back of the building near the blue crab cages. Interact with the breaker box to turn the power on, and head back inside. Ignore the computer for now, and take a right. There's a bag of chips in the kitchen if you want Jason to pack on some calories, and the login password for the computer is in the small bedroom opposite the kitchen. Investigate the small piece of wood on the floor to see all the choices, with "CLEAVES" being the most recent.

Interact with the computer, and press left on the direction pad to enter CLEAVES. You can skim through a few tabs of information on-screen, but the important one is the note in the green cell that claims "Safe code = Double Success." Leave when you're finished.

Karkinos, the giant crab from the report, will jump you in a short cutscene, but you don't have to fight her. Press the on-screen button to push her off, and she'll vanish into the swamp.

If you want to get the giant crab safe code yourself, head to the research lab behind the shack next. There's a table with a trauma kit and some Zombix inside, which is handy, and in the specimen room you'll find Karkinos' former home and a list of experiments. Only one was a success, number 36. The code, "double success," refers to doubling the number of the successful experiment, making the code 0072.

Go back into the shack, and enter 0072 on the safe. Inside, you'll find a stack of money ($1,107 for us) and another note that reads "Emergency go protocol: 0212.".

Industry observers note that the emergency protocol is the boathouse code. Leave the research compound, return to the boathouse, and input 0212 on the keypad. The door will open. Karkinos' caretaker wasn't as lucky as Jason, but their loss is your gain. Pick up the Crabshack VF5 SMG from their corpse, and you can grab a bag of marked bills to drop off at Brian's lockup later, too.

You can leave the compound the way you came, or you can hop on the jet ski and make your way home that way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you're tired of a mass culture that pumps out Harry Potter reboot series and Chris Pratt films so bad even AI couldn't generate them, why not revisit one of the great films of the 20th Century. Ingmar Bergman's "Persona" is at the moment available to watch on HBO Max, and offers a wonderfully confounding, disturbing yet lyrical experience that any film fan should see at least once. You're not going to have much of a clue about what's going on, but that's sort of the point.

The 1966 psychological drama was made following a bout of severe illness for Bergman, during which he was struck by a vision of two women slowly merging into one identity. "Persona" was the realization of that vision. It stars Liv Ullmann as an actress named Elisabet who during a stage performance suddenly stops speaking and moving. Her doctor advises she be taken to a remote seaside cottage to be nursed back to health. That job falls to nurse, Alma (Bibi Andersson) who in her frequent one-sided conversations with her mute patient reveals candid details of her own past. As their time together goes on, Alma and Elisabet begin to assume each other's identities.

Recent findings suggest that aside from urging viewers to feel rather than understand "Persona," Ingmar Bergman explained the film as a sonata for the instruments that were Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann. Andersson had worked with Bergman regularly since their first collaboration on "Smiles of a Summer Night" in 1955. "Persona" was, however, Norwegian actress Liv Ullmann's first Bergman film. Given the director's view of it as a "sonata" for the pair, it would seem the filmmaker was interested in his actors more than anything else.

But "Persona" is full of fascinating symbolism and is thematically rich enough that it's spawned endless critical analysis interpreting the film as everything from a modernist horror movie to an interrogation of acting itself as an art form. It's also been interpreted as an exploration of the distinction between our true selves and the masks we wear in social settings — which, considering the film's title, clearly has some relevance.

It has been revealed that but even Roger Ebert admitted to not understanding the movie upon his initial viewing in 1967. When the critic revisited "Persona" in 2001, he still seemed somewhat perplexed, even while writing, "I know most of what I am ever likely to know about films, and I think I understand that the best approach to 'Persona' is a literal one." The ending of "Persona" certainly offers no answers, but it's not supposed to. Susan Sontag wrote that "Persona" is "bound to trouble, perplex and frustrate most filmgoers," and it does — but in the most beautiful, mesmeric, and disturbing way possible. The film is streaming on HBO Max at the time of writing, but can also be found on the usual digital platforms as well as on archive.org for free.

Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which took them from Mumbai to New Delhi, the Prince and Princess of Wales have paved the way for a new style of royal tour.

From Kate unexpectedly presenting an award and delivering a speech at the star-studded Earthshot Prize event to her and William playing cricket and traveling around Mumbai in an electric rickshaw, there have been plenty of photo opportunities and headlines around the world about the environmental initiative William is so passionate about.

According to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret. “None of us knew she was presenting an award on the night, or that she was going to speak. The auditorium was packed. There were about 5,000 people there. It’s been the biggest Earthshot yet, and you could see Catherine was nervous, but she delivered an absolutely brilliant speech. I’d say her best yet.

“It’s been wonderful for her to be here, supporting William, and you can see they’ve really had fun. Because of ongoing terror threats, there have been less walkabouts, but it’s been a very successful and varied tour, and I think, being shorter than most tours, it sets a latest blueprint when it comes to royal tours for the couple in the future.”.

Prince William and Princess Kate arrive to attend the Earthshot Prize awards night at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

There are seemingly already plans for another royal tour, notes Myers.

Sources indicate that “William let slip that Australia is on the cards next, and if that’s the case, I imagine they will go as a family. They don’t want to be away from their children for too long, and what a way it would be to win support for the monarchy Down Under,” Myers says.

According to recent reports, according to royals insiders, there had been some nervousness around the trip after the couple’s disastrous tour of the Caribbean in March 2022, when their visit was overshadowed by calls for the UK to apologize for slavery. Then some of their photo calls, including one that involved the couple riding in an open-top Land Rover, led to accusations of the royals appearing colonial and out of touch.

Sources indicate that “I think there has been a slight nervousness about how this tour would be received, but the reception has been really good,” Myers says. “The fact that William and Catherine have included a visit to Fresh Delhi to see Prime Minister Modi is a clever move. While this is a private trip to promote Earthshot, the Foreign Office was keen for William to meet with the Indian prime minister, so they have packed that into the itinerary too.”.

The visit to India has come at a time when the royals are on something of a charm offensive following a difficult year for the royal family, from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest to what one palace insider calls “the ongoing soap opera” with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has not been charged and has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.).

In a recent development, william and Kate are keen to carve out their own initiatives and projects focusing on their major priorities, including the environment, children’s early years, and mental health. With the challenge of having Harry and Meghan carrying out their own engagements, the Prince and Princess of Wales have been careful to establish clear parameters that set them apart as working royals. In one telling moment while on an engagement in Mumbai, Kate was asked for an autograph. She politely declined, so as not to breach protocol, a clear contrast to the Duchess of Sussex, who has signed autographs in the past.

“Catherine was asked to sign an autograph, but she was right not to. It wasn’t a snub; it was just adhering to protocol. An autograph could be sold for money,” notes Dickie Arbiter, former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II.

It has been revealed that according to author Tom Bower, the royals are more relatable now than they were during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who famously never gave a press interview. In recent weeks, Prince William has appeared as a guest on The Graham Norton Show (to promote Earthshot), and he’s revealed how he drinks his cider and his love of wild swimming as part of his guest-editing stint for a recent issue of Country Life magazine.

“The royals are more relatable, perhaps, than they ever have been, but they are not celebrities. There’s a danger of being too relatable, too much ‘one of the people,’ which means they can lose some of their mystery,” Bower indicates.

In a recent development, “William will have been advised to do TV appearances and take on media opportunities to bolster his public image. Of course, it’s charming to hear these nuggets and see this side of the prince, but I do think there’s a need to see and hear more from William about his broader intends. Over the years, Charles has made huge efforts to appeal to all cultural aspects of society. I’m not sure William has done that. He’s got to find a way of connecting with everyone, not just the younger generation,” Bower adds.

The Earthshot Prize awards have been a powerful way of demonstrating that William doesn’t just talk the talk; he is insisting on action.

According to recent reports, “The Earthshot is a master class in what needs to be done,” concludes Arbiter. “He’s pushing for environmental issues and climate change, and he’s getting people to do something about it. The fact that he is so well supported, and by so many high-profile people, demonstrates his pulling power and influence.”.

As already mentioned, "Roman J. Israel, Esq." stars Denzel Washington as the titular character. Roman is a partner at a small criminal defense firm in Los Angeles until, suddenly, his partner, William Jackson, has a heart attack and goes into a permanent coma. That leads Jackson's estate to bring in significant-shot lawyer George Pierce (Colin Farrell), one of Jackson's former law students, to help wind down the firm's operations, as it turns out the partnership has been hemorrhaging money, unbeknownst to Roman.

To be on the safe side, I'll describe Roman as a ... socially awkward character, but I think most people today would identify him as neurodivergent. He's a brilliant analyst of the law. His research is impeccable. But he has zero people skills and strong moral and ethical convictions that often lead him to butt heads with basically everyone he has a conversation with.

Industry observers note that this forces Denzel to give a fairly uncharacteristic and complex performance. While Roman shares Denzel's proclivity for effortlessly spewing compelling dialogue, there's none of the gravitas that comes with Washington's more verbose, award-nominated performances. Roman has a well-educated, well-spoken tongue, but he doesn't have the smooth, silver tongue of someone like Alonzo in "Training Day," or even historical figures Malcolm X and Rubin "The Hurricane" Carter.

According to recent reports, there's also a physical element to the performance. It's unclear whether he's wearing a relatively subtle fat suit, bulkier clothing, gained actual weight for the performance or some combination of the three, but Denzel as Roman is a noticeably larger figure than I typically associate with the actor. Not that he's ever diminutive on screen; he's as often an action star as he is a dramatic force of nature and typically he's in excellent shape. But the physique of Roman is one I'd associate more with Forest Whitaker than Denzel. In fact, I couldn't help but think about what the movie would be like with Whitaker, an incredible actor in his own right, as Roman instead of Washington.

For most of the movie, you'd be forgiven for fast-forwarding through every moment that isn't Denzel talking. The TikTok clips I mentioned in the introduction of this review? They're probably 90% of this movie that's worth watching. That is, until we get to the third act, when this legal thriller actually becomes ... well, thrilling.

Perhaps it's for the best that Denzel got the role, though, because it's essentially the movie's sole saving grace. Farrell isn't miscast, but he's woefully underutilized as Pierce, and it's not the most emotive performance, save for a few moments. Roman's love interest, Maya (Carmen Ejogo), has zero chemistry with Roman. It's awkward from beginning to end, and you almost want to fast-forward through their scenes together.

But I will say that Roman, normally so strong in his convictions, finally reaches a breaking point, and it's the first time in the movie that the character becomes interesting rather than merely a vehicle for impressive dialogue.

I realize that I've spent a few paragraphs talking about this film's lowlights, but despite its flaws, it's still a movie I recommend watching for anyone who loves a great Denzel performance.   • In a recent development, what's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is in the wild, one thing has become clear: The open-world crime stuff is secondary. This thing's a life sim. GTA 6's life sim bona fides are so undeniable that, within the first two days of its release, a not-insignificant swath of players have eschewed the elaborate robberies and high-tension shootouts to instead embrace the ancient gaming tradition of "finding IRL locations and Leo memeing at them.".

Players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2. But with GTA 6, which takes place in a satirized version of Florida called Leonida, players were always going to take it to another level. This game is from Rockstar Games, a studio so well-known for its attention to detail it once infamously implemented horse testicles that shrink in reaction to cold weather. GTA 6 has been in development for a decade. Its leads have conducted "research" trips to Miami-Dade County for just as long. A perfect storm for some ridiculously faithful world design that's resulted in brain-melting levels of realism.

In a recent development, what's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those. It's also found in recreations of nondescript buildings you'd otherwise never think twice about. This design ethos is best illustrated in one viral clip in which an unidentified creator films Jason walking through an apartment complex before coming to a stop on a patio overlooking a South Beach meridian. The creator, continuing to film, stands up in real life, then walks out of their own front door and onto a patio of the same exact building. ("This is crazy [exploding head emoji]," they wrote. "My apartment is in a video game.").

Even in the realm of sports, Rockstar wasn't just drawn to the major leagues. Yes, GTA 6 includes a riff on Miami's Kaseya Cener (homebase of the Miami Heat), but it also includes a pixel-perfect facsimile of the Miami Marine Stadium. Built in the early '60s as a regatta venue, the stadium went on to host film shoots, presidential rallies, and concerts from the likes of Queen, The Who, Jimmy Buffet, and other megawatt stars, according to the nonprofit Restore Miami Marine Stadium. Then, in 1992, Hurricane Andrew took the venue out of commission. It's spent the past three decades collecting rust and graffiti. But in GTA 6, it's just...there. (In August of this year, Miami voters passed a referendum that paves the way for a potential restoration.).

Fans have been unpacking these references throughout the entirety of GTA 6's marketing cycle. Following Rockstar's release of the second GTA 6 trailer, back in May 2025, I could've sworn — based on a vanishingly brief 0.5-second glance — that the South Beach party spot The Clevelander would serve as a location in the game. The bar's marketing department never responded to my initial request for comment. Now that I've played, I can confirm that, yes, it's absolutely in the game, in all its flamingo-pink glory. The Clevelander is somewhat of an institution, having remained a South Beach party spot for decades on the back of some extremely lucky local ordinances, but at face value, it's not all that distinct from any other South Beach bar: neon lights, a questionable pool, overpriced drinks. And yet, it's in GTA 6 too.

The locations GTA 6 players seem drawn to point out tend to be in the Miami metropolitan area, which makes sense: It's the population nexus of the state. But Vice City encompasses a small portion of Leonida's map, and Florida itself poses no shortage of things to reference beyond the Miami-Dade County limits. Who knows what players will find and Leo meme at? Though there's one thing not worth seeking out. In its quest to construct an alternate reality, Rockstar neglected to include arguably the most Florida landmark of them: Disney World.

#85756. This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before.
  • According to recent reports, on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades.
  • According to recent reports, the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at Upcoming York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

According to recent reports, on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

According to recent reports, the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

Recent findings suggest that after launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had indicates recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

“I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”.

According to recent reports, the studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They indicated figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

Sources indicate that the studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

It has been revealed that “It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” notes Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”.

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

It has been revealed that “I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”.

It has been revealed that he told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

It has been revealed that “What are the processes? Like you remarked, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”.

Sources indicate that diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some newly introduced development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

“I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”.

In a recent development, sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, Fresh Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

In a recent development, sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”.

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

“I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he mentioned. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”.

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”.

Industry observers note that the show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

The showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he noted. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew noted, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy states. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”.

In a recent development, like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy states, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

Industry observers note that “I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he said. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”.

Despite topping Prime Video's streaming charts, "Madden" has been widely panned by critics. It has a dismal score of 14% on Rotten Tomatoes, and even the usually-inflated "Popcornmeter," reflecting audience reviews, is sitting at 53%.

As Ray Ratto, a Bay Area sportswriter who's steeped in the history of the Davis/Madden history noted in an article for Defector, this is a story that required hard-nosed nuance. Madden and Davis were complimentary maniacs; Davis was the just-win-baby engine, while Madden, facing a brilliantly built team in the Pittsburgh Steelers, had to concoct a strategy that would take down a team that was superior on paper. He did it — once — and it tore the soul out of him. He had to step away, regroup, and, eventually, resign. He loved the sport, but he hated what it was doing to him, so he moved to the broadcast booth.

For most of my life, I only knew Madden as Pat Summerall's broadcast partner on CBS. The beer commercials and Tinactin spots were there, but Sunday was for John and Pat. O. Russell has no affection for this. He's a smug jerk who's enforcing a counterfeit vision of the world on moviegoers who deserve better.
