  • Sources indicate that you see, one of the joys of live theater is bearing witness to a performer who's captured the music of an uncommonly gifted playwright's dialogue.
  • Lonergan remembered this and cast Ruffalo in his 2000 film classic "You Can Count on Me." Then, when the actor started booking studio gigs, Lonergan cooked up "Margaret." It's a Latest York City epic about a teenager (Anna Paquin) who struggles to cope with a fatal city bus accident she inadvertently put in motion, with Ruffalo playing the bus driver whose ill-advised, but innocuous, flirtation leads to a horrible accident on the Upper West Side of Manhattan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What a difference seven-odd months make. Near the tail-end of September 2011, Fox Searchlight dumped Kenneth Lonergan's "Margaret" six years after it was filmed, only for its star, Mark Ruffalo, to Hulk-out in "The Avengers" the following May. But even so, Lonergan's movie — one of the best of the 21st Century — deserves so much better than to merely be remembered as a box office bomb.

Sources indicate that you see, one of the joys of live theater is bearing witness to a performer who's captured the music of an uncommonly gifted playwright's dialogue. In my lifetime, I've seen Philip Seymour Hoffman and John C. Reilly make a meal out of Sam Shepard's "True West," Rosemary Harris and Elaine Stritch tear up Edward Albee's "A Delicate Balance," and Jeffrey Wright and Don Cheadle set the stage ablaze with Suzan-Lori Parks' "Topdog/Underdog." On that same level, a late-20-something Ruffalo caused an off-Broadway stir in the fall of 1996 with his portrayal of troubled teenager Walter Straub in Lonergan's finely wrought drama "This Is Our Youth." He exuded shaggily handsome charm as a purposeless kid with a short-term game plan that involves absconding with $15,000 of his wealthy dirtbag father's money.

Lonergan remembered this and cast Ruffalo in his 2000 film classic "You Can Count on Me." Then, when the actor started booking studio gigs, Lonergan cooked up "Margaret." It's a Latest York City epic about a teenager (Anna Paquin) who struggles to cope with a fatal city bus accident she inadvertently put in motion, with Ruffalo playing the bus driver whose ill-advised, but innocuous, flirtation leads to a horrible accident on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. This is as close to a clean logline as you can get with Lonergan's rich, sophisticated text, which baffled its dilettante, bigoted, multi-millionaire producer Gary Gilbert.

In a recent development, "Margaret" was a talent magnet. Kenneth Lonergan's blisteringly brilliant screenplay drew in Mark Ruffalo, Paquin, Matt Damon, J. Smith Cameron, Allison Janney, Matthew Broderick, Jean Reno, and Rosemarie DeWitt. The great Jeannie Berlin, a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nominee for her knockout work in 1972's "The Heartbreak Kid," also appeared in the movie (her first since 1990's "In the Spirit"), and she was dubbed Best Supporting Actress by the Village Voice Film Poll for her turn as the sister of the victim killed in the aforementioned accident.

"Margaret" is a drama without villains. Anna Paquin's Lisa is a misguided and impulsive teenager. She is in search of justice where nothing of the sort can be found and tracks down Ruffalo's bus driver. He's well aware of the threat she poses to his steady bus-driving job, though, and shoos her away. But she persists, and her version of the events of that deadly day aren't entirely wrong, yet she still shares some responsibility. Yet, she can't accept that, so her catharsis will not arrive via a conviction.

According to recent reports, structurally, "Margaret" splits its time between Lisa's errant pursuit of justice and her mother (Cameron) as she tries to connect with a suave suitor played by Reno. Everyone loses. But this loss forges a stronger bond between mother and daughter. It binds them anew during a Lincoln Center performance of "The Tales of Hoffman," where, wordlessly, they patch up their wounds. (Heal? No. Those scabs will always be pickable.).

Industry observers note that it would be nice if a movie like that could go toe-to-toe with something on the level of "The Avengers," but there it is. Still, if you only really know Lonergan for his Oscar-winning "Manchester by the Sea," make it a priority to finally watch "Margaret.".

From a gown purchased with wartime rations to a secret engraving on the ring: Inside the historic royal wedding of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple.
  • November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.
  • The Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.

The Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was stated to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

The couple on their engagement, 1947.

In 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately stated yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.

Princess Elizabeth with Philip Mountbatten on their wedding day.

The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

According to recent reports, like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

Designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

Princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

According to recent reports, as Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”.

Princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, noted to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

In a recent development, all royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.

Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.

The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.

The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.

Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.

Recent findings suggest that the wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip walking down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, followed by their bridesmaids and pages.

Recent findings suggest that there were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

Together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.).

The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”.

The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

On the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.

The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.

During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.

The couple waving from the balcony of Buckingham Palace.

Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

Although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.

Mr Schur, chief confectioner at McVitie and Price, putting the final touches to the wedding cake.

The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

In a recent development, over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.

The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip being showered with rose petals as they leave Buckingham Palace, London, for their honeymoon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After more than a decade of waiting, it seems we may finally get a newly introduced theatrically released Star Trek movie. While dedicated Trekkies have heard that before, the directors of the only known Star Trek movie in development recently shared details about their project. The pair helming the new Trek film, Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley, broke down the movie's influences in an interview with Inverse.

Specifically, they cited Training Day and Crimson Tide as jumping-off points for what they’re going for.

In a recent development, for those unfamiliar with Training Day, it stars Ethan Hawke as a newcomer LAPD narcotics officer under the tutelage of the corrupt detective Alonzo Harris, played by Denzel Washington. As for Crimson Tide, it’s a thriller about a U.S. nuclear submarine facing off against a Russian ultranationalist faction threatening to launch nukes at the U.S. and Japan (interestingly enough, it also stars Washington).

In a recent development, as for how the Training Day influence will show up in the film, Daley said the movie will center on some of the “bad apples” in Starfleet. “I would say it’s really kind of a look at the institution of Starfleet and any institution as a whole that has existed for a long time and what that does,” Daley said to Inverse. “I think the portrayal of Starfleet and the people that work within it have always been generally idealized versions of what the future could be. And while this [script] isn’t a cynical or nihilistic take on it, I think it does acknowledge that there are some bad apples in every institution that can have a strong voice and can really make an impact on that institution and everything it stands for.”.

Sources indicate that past Star Trek movies have dealt with Starfleet bad apples before to varying levels of success, including Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country, Star Trek: Insurrection, and Star Trek Into Darkness. But Daly and Goldstein have another twist on the Star Trek formula.

“It takes place almost in real time, and it just is a whole other look at what a Star Trek movie could be without betraying the fundamentals of what it should be,” Daley said.

The pair added that the film will center on all-latest Star Trek characters. “I mean, look, we don’t want to rely on fandom,” Goldstein remarked. “We don’t want to just hope that there’s enough fans of the original [TOS] or The Next Generation or whatever who will turn out for this. We want to just make a great movie that lives in the world that people are familiar with — some people are familiar with — and that others will discover. And then, with good fortune, we launch a new franchise into existence.”.

Sources indicate that although the film is still only in development, there are reasons to be excited based on Daley and Goldstein’s recent work. The pair previously co-directed and co-wrote the surprisingly fun Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, which starred former James T. Kirk actor Chris Pine. Before that, they co-directed the action comedy Game Night, and their most recent theatrical release, Mayday, also received positive reviews.

Without Daley and Goldstein’s film, Star Trek would unfortunately be at risk of going on ice for a bit. Besides Star Trek: Strange Latest Worlds and Starfleet Academy, both of which will end after their next seasons, there aren’t any revealed TV series in the works. Hopefully, this movie can get the franchise back in Paramount’s good graces.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, there is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the starship Enterprise first rolled out its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world. Astronaut Mae Jemison, for example, credited Nichelle Nichols' performance as Lt. Uhura with inspiring her to become the first African-American woman to make it into space. Even the flip phones of the '90s were at least partially inspired by the design of the communicators on the original "Trek.".

In a recent development, there is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in. That's right: "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was the first movie to be featured in a Happy Meal.

Long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families. McDonald's executives liked the idea and hired advertiser Bob Bernstein, who decided to bundle those smaller portions into a box that would feature bright, kid-friendly colors and a small toy to keep the youngsters entertained while mom and dad threw down on their Big Macs. Thus, the Happy Meal was born, and after being tested in 1977, it rolled out nationwide in 1979.

Sources indicate that needless to say, it was a hit with customers, but the last piece of this familiar fry-scented puzzle would come at the end of the year, when "Star Trek" was revived for the significant screen with the entire main cast of the show returning to their roles. When the film ran over budget during production — not to mention injuries and other problems plaguing the set — Paramount's Vice President of Marketing and Licensing, Dawn Steel, was tasked with figuring out how to cover some of the rapidly expanding costs. She went looking for brand partners, and apparently someone at McDonald's was enough of a Trekkie to go for it. This approach was so successful that it would become almost mandatory for blockbuster movies to have some sort of fast-food tie-in as the years went on, a marketing tactic that would even change the direction of entire franchises, like it did with the infamous "Batman Returns" tie-in.

Looking back, doing a Happy Meal tie-in for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was, well, kind of a weird choice. As much as "Trek" had become a cultural touchstone due to the popularity of syndicated re-runs after its original three-season run, the film is a pretty slow, ponderous affair. It's largely about negotiating with a sentient space cloud, punctuated with bits of action like the scene where two members of the ship's crew die screaming for almost a full minute in a transporter accident. It's not a particularly gory or violent movie and there's nothing too objectionable, but it's not exactly "Bambi" — which would get its own Happy Meal tie-in in 1988 — either.

Sources indicate that it's especially funny to think about the movie's slow-paced meditations on the unknown and the toll of aging in the context of the Happy Meal itself. Considering that the ad for the Happy Meal involved a Klingon yelling things like "yum-yum" and laughing at the jokes printed on the boxes, they might have given kids a bit of an unrealistic idea of what they were going to get at the movie theater.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I knew it had become increasingly rare for Hollywood productions to actually be filmed in Los Angeles, but Rob Lowe’s stats for The Floor really put things into perspective. The host of the Fox game show, which is on the 2026 TV schedule this fall season, just got real about why it’s filmed all the way in Ireland rather than at the network’s own lot. And, wow!

Recent findings suggest that ever since The Floor premiered back in 2023, the game show featuring 100 contestants, a giant LED floor grid and a $250,000 grand prize has been made in Ireland. When Lowe was asked why he shoots it overseas, he mentioned this:.

Industry observers note that when people want to know how bad the economics are in California, and Los Angeles in particular in terms of the industry that created this town. It is more cost-efficient to find 100 Americans and bring them to Ireland and shoot the game show in Ireland than it is to shoot in the soundstages [on the Fox lot] right outside the window of the offices where we’re trying to figure out what we’re going to do next season.

Yeah, this really illustrates the rough situation in LA right now. When I looked deeper into it, I found out that there are a few factors that probably played into The Floor deciding to go to Ireland rather than stay in Los Angeles. One is the rigid labor regulations in Los Angeles that just don’t apply in Ireland. Another is how much more expensive it would be for the production to board the one hundred contestants during the shoots. And then, there’s the competitive tax incentives Ireland has in place to encourage productions to be there. Lowe continued with these words:.

Sources indicate that there’s a new California initiative that did pass to help bring production back into LA. And then, there's also a national one that people are talking about. But, that would still only make it competitive with some of the other [markets]. I mean, it’s 40% less expensive, 40. It’s a lot of money.

It sounds like The Floor just wouldn’t be able to exist if it were shot in Los Angeles. There are a number of TV reveals that currently shoot in the City of Angels, like Dancing With The Stars, The Pitt, The Rookie, 911, Shrinking and Abbott Elementary, and some incentives in California are starting to help repair the market. However, as Lowe also shared while on Mostly Sheenius, there’s a long way to go before it becomes cost-efficient again. As he put it:.

It is definitely trending up, but it is trending up from the basement of where it used to be.

Tons of Los Angeles TV shows recently moved to new locations, such as Shark Tank and American Idol moving to Atlanta and The Masked Singer to New Jersey. It’s also been reported lately (per Deadline) that America’s Got Talent is scouting a new home outside of its longtime home in Pasadena, California.

The Floor airs new episodes on Wednesdays (with the finale airing on December 2). If you’re looking to catch up on the new season, you can do so now with either a Disney+ subscription and/or a Hulu subscription. Lowe’s explanation of why The Floor shoots in Ireland kind of blows my mind, but as a Los Angeles resident, I totally see how expensive it is over here, too. Hopefully some of these incentives will change things because so much of the workforce over here relies on the entertainment industry.

Recent findings suggest that since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, upcoming Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

Léa Seydoux and Daniel Craig pose as they arrive on the set of No Time To Die on September 09, 2019 in Matera, Italy.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she stated with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”.

In a recent development, when pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux remarked. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”.

The online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

Bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”.

Recent findings suggest that denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”.

Industry observers note that it's almost time to close out 2026, so there are only a handful of new episodes of "Saturday Night Live" left this year. NBC's staple late night sketch comedy show is at the moment in the middle of Season 52, and they're coming off quite a celebrated episode after comedian John Mulaney returned to host for a seventh time. Mulaney has become one of the most reliable returning hosts, which is why he's also one of the best "SNL" hosts of all time.

According to recent reports, but that's in the past, and "SNL" is always looking ahead to the next show. As we head into the busy holiday season, you're probably wondering when you can take a break and catch some laughs with a newly introduced episode of "SNL." Plus, you don't have time to wait and see whether there's a new episode when Saturday night rolls around. That's why we're here to let you know if there's a new "SNL" on November 21, 2026, as well as keep you posted on what's coming up next for "SNL.".

There is no new episode of "SNL" on November 21, 2026.

In a recent development, john Mulaney's episode was the last of three consecutive episodes running from Halloween through mid-November, and it's rare that executive producer Lorne Michaels pushes the cast and crew to do more than that in a row, as the series is truly exhausting to produce each week. (You can learn more about how the show is produced through a series of "SNL" documentaries available on Peacock that chronicle exactly how the show's team makes it happen over and over again.).

You would do well to check out John Mulaney's episode, if you haven't already, because it delivered the best episode of the season, including this sketch that every family is probably fighting about:.

Plus, let's not forget that Mulaney delivered what has now become a traditional Latest York-based musical sketch, including a special guest appearance by former cast member Bowen Yang:.

Since Thanksgiving is coming up, "SNL" is taking a short break before returning for several more episodes in December. Speaking of which...

In a recent development, "SNL" will be back with a fresh episode on December 5. More than likely, we'll get another three episodes in a row before Lorne Michaels gives the cast and crew their traditional holiday break over Christmas and through New Year into mid-to-late January. There's a chance we might only get two, since the third Saturday would be December 19, and that's pretty close to Christmas, but we don't know for sure yet.

When "SNL" returns on December 5, the episode will be hosted be someone who has been drumming up a lot of buzz, thanks to their appearance in a highly discussed movie that's still in theaters now.

Amanda Seyfried will be making her hosting debut on the December 5 episode. Yes, this is the first time Seyfried has hosted the show. In fact, this is the first time she'll be making any appearance on "SNL," having never previously made a cameo in other episodes. But she's proven to be funny in comedies like "Mean Girls" and "Ted 2" (pictured above) over the years, so we're excited to see what she can do on "SNL.".

Seyfried is presently riding high after a (SPOILER ALERT) riveting appearance in "You Can See Everything," the documentary from directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder that follows convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares to serve her federal prison sentence. Seyfried's role in the movie is so compelling and unique that some are wondering if there's potential for her to get a Best Supporting Actress nomination (she partakes in pivotal reenactments that help define the movie's fascinating framework and revelations).

In addition, Seyfried voices Cinderella in an animated Netflix movie called "Steps," hitting the streaming service starting on November 20, and she also stars in "The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd," a fresh movie written and directed by actor Tim Blake Nelson. The latter has been playing film festivals across the country, but it's not clear if it will be given an awards qualifying release in theaters otherwise before the end of 2026.

Seyfried will be joined by musical guest Don Toliver, a rapper whose fifth studio release, "Octane," became his first number one album this year.

"SNL" typically starts at 11:30pm ET, though that can potentially get disrupted by live sporting events or breaking news, which can delay the show slightly. However, in those cases, the show still unfolds live, but it's tape-delayed for those who will be watching "live" on NBC and/or Peacock.

When "SNL" is airing live, you can watch either on NBC through your usual television provider or by streaming live through Peacock.

Sources indicate that don't worry if you're not at home when the show starts at 11:30pm ET. NBC uploads new sketches to YouTube not long after their air live. Plus, full new episodes are available to watch on Peacock the next day.

It has been revealed that in addition, Peacock holds a library of old "SNL" episodes from across the show's decades-spanning history. However, those episodes don't always have all the sketches or musical performances due to complicated licensing rights for music.

For those who might like a little comedic flavor from across the pond, there's also "Saturday Night Live UK." Though you can't easily watch live here in the United States, new episodes of "SNL UK" hit Peacock on Sunday evenings the day after new episodes air.

After you watch the latest episode of "SNL," be sure to check out "The Ten to One Podcast," featuring me as one of the hosts recapping and reviewing new episodes of "SNL.".

8 Must-Play JRPGs for People With Real-Life Schedules

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s 9:15 on a Wednesday night.
  • But there are some games in the genre you can bend to fit your week.
  • According to recent reports, how do you finish an RPG that can run past 100 hours when you have only 30 spare minutes — on a good night?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s 9:15 on a Wednesday night. The dishes are done. You have about 45 minutes before bed, and you’re a JRPG fan (or you were, when you had more time). JRPGs tend to demand dozens of hours from players — and they can make it very difficult to pause, as some of them will interrupt you with a battle every few steps.

But there are some games in the genre you can bend to fit your week. These eight JRPGs split their stories into chapters, let you switch off random battles, speed up fights, or save almost anywhere. Even if you press start at 9:20, you can still be in bed by 10.

According to recent reports, how do you finish an RPG that can run past 100 hours when you have only 30 spare minutes — on a good night? Dragon Quest 11: Echoes of an Elusive Age can do it, as long as you play it in small pieces. You’re the Luminary, a silent hero raised in the village of Cobblestone who learns he's the reincarnation of a legendary hero destined to fight the Dark One. Your trip across the bright, friendly land of Erdrea builds a party one self-contained chapter at a time, each with its own local problems to solve. To make this big game work in small doses, pick either 3D mode or 2D mode and stay there. (Progress carries over poorly when you switch.) You can also raise the battle speed, which can make fights up to three times faster and cuts down on grinding. Then save at a Sacred Stone, and treat each stop as a chapter break.

This game opens with a disaster: the Great Chasm swallows a village, and a shepherd named Tiz is the only survivor. You play as Tiz, who teams up with Agnes, a vestal of the Wind Crystal, to free four elemental crystals that darkness has swallowed. Edea, a defector from the Eternian Sky Knights, and Ringabel, an amnesiac who carries a journal that seems to record future events, join the party along the way.

This remaster explicitly hands you the controls for your schedule. You can set the encounter rate from 50 to 200 percent at any time on the field map, push battle speed to 4x, and let auto-battle repeat your last actions. Turn the dial to match whatever time and energy you happen to have when you’re ready to play.

Time to beat: Between 15-30 hours per game.

Random battles are the reason many people bounce off old JRPGs. The Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster series gives you a switch for those random encounters, so — problem solved. The series remasters Final Fantasy 1 through 6 in 2D pixel art. Start with the first game, where four heroes of light must save the world by recovering four elemental crystals from castles, towers, and mountains. As you wend your way through the game’s dungeons, pull up the Boost menu. With it, you can turn random encounters on or off at any time and raise EXP, gil, and ability point gains up to four times. When your four heroes need levels before the next crystal, raise the EXP boost and turn encounters back on. Switch encounters off, walk to the next town, and get your evening back.

Art aficionados-slash-JRPG-fans rejoice: This game’s distinctive 160-plus locations are handmade dioramas that were photographed and converted into 3D worlds. Here, you play Leo, an amnesiac who sets out to recover his memories while a mechanical infection called Mechteria spreads across the land. Hironobu Sakaguchi produced it and wrote the story. He also included a scheduling trick: the Dimengeon Machine. This machine stores the enemies you’ve already fought, so you can reach chests and save points without stopping for random encounters. It also fills rapidly late in the game, so empty it at the start of a long session and leave it on while you walk. Here’s your basic blueprint: Walk first, fight later.

A magical explosion ends a war between three kingdoms while killing thousands. A mercenary named Glenn sets out to find and destroy the crystal weapon behind the detonation. He’s joined by a princess who left her castle to see the world and a master thief . There are fights with mechs in their future. Lots of them.

In a recent development, chained Echoes is a 16-bit-style JRPG set on the continent of Valandis. While your characters are committed to fighting, you don’t have to be: This game allows you to skip random encounters, long treks to inns, and endless grinds. Enemies stay visible on the map, and your party recovers health between fights. You can save anywhere, and fast travel is free once the introductory sequence ends. Combat is turn-based and fast, and an Overdrive gauge keeps you thinking about which skills you use. Fight, save, and close the lid. Come back tomorrow (or whenever). Repeat.

Crono goes to the Millennial Fair and ends up four centuries in the past. (We’ve all been there.) During a friend’s scientific demonstration, a girl named Marle is pulled through a time rift, and Crono follows. His chase to save Marle becomes a quest to save the planet’s future, with stops in prehistory, the Middle Ages, the distant future, and the End of Time. Chrono Trigger is one of the shortest games here, at about 16-32 hours for the main story. The Steam version saves your progress both at dedicated save points and when you quit. It also saves automatically as you move around the map. Know that time does keep moving while you’re in a fight, so make sure to hit pause whenever life interrupts. As it turns out, saving the future is easier when you can pause the present, anyway.

On the continent of Orsterra, Ophilia the cleric takes her church's pilgrimage, Cyrus the scholar hunts for a vanished tome, and Tressa the merchant follows the author of an anonymous diary. Olberic, a former knight, takes up his sword again when bandits kidnap a boy. Primrose the dancer plots revenge, Alfyn the apothecary wants to ease suffering, Therion the thief needs three Dragonstones to win his freedom, and H'aanit the hunter searches for her missing master.

It has been revealed that each of the eight heroes’ stories has four chapters. Nearly every chapter follows the same loop: Enter a town, talk to people, clear a dungeon, beat a boss. That makes each boss fight your stopping point. Recommended-level gates mean you'll rotate between heroes, so no single story stalls. Save at the white feather icons near dungeons and towns. Play through one chapter whenever you have a free-ish night, and Orsterra will be yours before you know it.

Can’t commit to one long story? Try seven short ones. Live A Live sends seven heroes through seven eras: a martial artist entering a global fighting tournament in the present day, a conflicted agent in the twilight of Edo Japan, a wanderer with a bounty on his head in the Wild West, a psychic in the near future, a spaceship crew whose AI turns lethal, a martial arts master in Imperial China searching for a disciple, and cavemen in prehistory. Each of the seven core chapters stands alone, so you can play them in any order. The gameplay in each chapter varies a bit: One is a straight run of fights that takes about a half hour. Others are mini RPGs with random encounters and some grinding, so perhaps it’s best to save those for a weekend.

#85732. The Method-Dressing Madness Behind Mckenna Grace‘s 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Press Tour Looks

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2825 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Vanityfair ↗ Open Full Page

The Method-Dressing Madness Behind Mckenna Grace‘s 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Press Tour Looks

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances.
  • According to recent reports, with the newly introduced Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend.
  • In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances. Made a household term by Law Roach and Zendaya, method dressing is when actors wear looks that pay homage to the film or show they’re promoting: See Zendaya’s on-theme looks across red carpets for Dune, Spiderman, and The Odyssey for a slew of examples.

According to recent reports, with the newly introduced Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend. A super fan of the Suzanne Collins book series and their film adaptations, Grace—who plays District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner—took a hand in the styling for her press run, weaving easter eggs into every look. Her stylist, Molly Dickson, was up for the challenge of translating Grace’s deep-cut references into custom and archival looks from Monique Lhuillier, Gucci, Celine and more.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

In a recent development, molly Dickson: I went to college in Minnesota and my major was advertising. Two weeks before I graduated, I called my mom and stated, "I'm not into this. I don't wanna do advertising." She said, "Well, what do you wanna do?" I told her, "I wanna do fashion. I wanna go to New York." She said, "No, absolutely not.".

Recent findings suggest that right after I graduated, I went to LA, this was 2009 during the recession, and no one was hiring. I got an internship at Marie Claire in Latest York, and enrolled back into college to get school credit to intern at Hearst. I worked at Marie Claire as a market assistant for almost two years, and then I left and assisted Leslie Fremar for seven years. That's when I fell in love with celebrity. Then ten years ago, I went off on my own.

What would you say are your aesthetic influences as a stylist?

My personal style relates very similarly to Sadie Sink's style, very effortless. She always wants to be very comfortable and easy, never anything frilly or over the top. Just a simple, beautiful dress, and you let it speak for itself.

Mckenna is a major fan of the original film series, so it’s clear you’re pulling from there as influences when dressing her. Is it a collaborative process when coming to one of these referential looks?

She's obviously a very huge fan of the franchise. We actually started having conversations about this tour in April, which is very early to start having conversations. I could just sense her excitement around it. She started sending me mood boards, and I actually looked back today at the mood board and it was, it was a lot of Katniss Everdeen. It had Joanna on it, and it was filled with these really strong female characters from the franchise.

It has been revealed that what she really wanted to hit was Katniss’ wedding gown look and the Mockingjay look with the wings. I was really stumped on how to pull that off without making it overly costumey.

Mckenna kept asking, "What's going on with those?" I knew the vision, but I didn't know how to execute it. I was working with Keke Palmer and the designer Michael Ngo. He was making some cool music costumes for Keke, and I asked, "Michael, could you make this silver piece?" 'Cause I really had no idea how to get it done.

He said, “I don't think I can do that. You know what? Just give me a day, let me play around with it." That night, he said, "I figured it out." We got the piece and I thought, "Okay, it needs to be a wedding dress under,” so I reached out to all the bridal houses. I wanted it to be vintage because it would tell a pretty story. Monique [Lhuillier] ended up sending a ton of wedding gowns, and the day before Mckenna came in for the fitting, I actually tried the wedding dresses on myself with the silver piece.

I sent Mckenna five dresses, and the one that she ended up wearing, she remarked, "That's it. I don't even need to try anything else. That's the one I'm gonna wear." Then, it was a matter of finding the right event to wear it to because it’s pretty nice, very dramatic.

Industry observers note that she was in Paris for the Miu Miu show, and I brought it there because she had the Hunger Games Museum event. It was a whole conversation with her team, like, "Is it the right moment? Is it too much for this event?" Her PR said, "No, this is the perfect moment. It's the best way to kick off the tour." The response with the Hunger Games fans—I have never seen anything like it before, ever.

What was the experience of having her be such a big part of the styling process?

Recent findings suggest that it makes my job so fun because she is so passionate about it and she loves Hunger Games so much, even just finding subtle nods back to the movie. She would say, "I wanna do a ladybug look." Thom Browne did that amazing ladybug dress, I thought, "That's so cool, but it's not really her personal aesthetic." So it’s finding ways to keep it still true to her personal style while maintaining the nods to the film.

The way you seem to understand Mckenna feels something similar to the connection between Katniss and Cinna in The Hunger Games. When pulling looks for her, what comes into play? How do you make her come through and not be lost in the lore of the stories or the dress?

Sources indicate that mckenna had remarked that she maybe wanted to do a red or a dark pink feather look because in the books [Maysilee] gets attacked by the red birds which are like flamingos. I'm pulling in all these red feather dresses and on the runway, this one dress looked amazing. Mckenna said, “That's perfect for the flamingo reference.”.

But we put it on her and it was so major, and she's so petite so she was just getting swarmed. I remarked, “Let"s not force it.” The goal was for her to feel comfortable in the look rather than just getting each reference.

The public has been really excited about these looks. Are you thinking about the response to the looks when you’re putting them together?

There's been some conversations in a fitting, like, "Oh, the Hunger Games fans are gonna get this." They're gonna see the inspiration, they're gonna understand it.

But I wouldn't say we're choosing a look because ‘Oh, this is gonna go viral to the Hunger Games community.’ Mckenna is a super fan herself so if she's getting excited about the look, everyone else that's a fan of the franchise is gonna get excited about the look.

Mckenna Grace in Betsey Johnson.

Do you feel any pressure to top the last outfit after each premiere?

In a recent development, yes. I think it was Paris because that wedding dress did get so much press. In that fitting, it felt like, "We gotta keep our game up high." It's been really fun for my team and market assistants because a lot of the girls that work with me are huge fans of the movie. They're not even seeing it as work. They're like, "Oh my God, this is so exciting. Look at this. This looks like this from the movie.".

What was the inspiration to do method dressing for this press run? What do you think is the value?

Mckenna knew back in April, she noted, "I wanna do method for this." I personally did not read the books. I'm a visual person, so I've seen all the movies. Lionsgate was able to let me go with the cast when they first saw the movie because my agent was like, "Molly needs to go to the movie to get inspired before this press tour. She can't do a method dressing press tour without seeing the movie.".

Even as the tour was going on, Mckenna kept sending me upcoming references and quotes from the book and stuff like that.

In a recent development, what made you take it to the next level? From paying homage to not only characters, but the actual actors from the films like Jennifer Lawrence at the 2011 Oscars to even dressing like set pieces from the film.

Sources indicate that that was all Mckenna's vision. On her first mood board, she had a lot of Jennifer Lawrence's red carpet moments because she's such a huge fan of Katniss and Jennifer Lawrence.

It has been revealed that with the Rue reference, Mckenna thought that color was just very Hunger Games. It wasn't until she put the dress on, her mom said, "Wait, this is Rue's dress." So that was just fate. I would love to take credit for that.

Why do you think that this styling has generated so much attention?

I think it’s when you do method dressing for such a substantial franchise and you really are passionate about it. The thing is that Mckenna is so excited and passionate about this movie. She has mentioned, “I didn't think that I would love doing fittings so much. I used to hate doing fittings.”.

Mckenna Grace in Elisabetta Franchi.

Because every look is so intentionally tied back to Hunger Games and she's such a major fan, it's literally like playing dress up with her. I think the fans see it, she's so relatable because she's a fan that all these fans think, "Wow, like, she's a fan and she got to do this." She’s the fangirl living out her dream, and the fans are excited for her that she finally gets to do this.

It has been revealed that what do you think are the best kinds of projects to implement method dressing with/works best with? What does it work best with?

According to recent reports, I think the big movies that already have a fan base, like Barbie or Wednesday, Being able to pull inspiration from existing books or films makes it so much easier for a stylist rather than a movie that no one's seen before. There's no curiosity or momentum about it because you're starting from scratch, whereas Hunger Games, Barbie, Wednesday, there's already a level of expectation.

The looks for this press run have been a mix of archival, upcoming, and custom pieces. How do you make that choice? How important is it for you to create an archive for Mckenna?

In a recent development, it kind of is a mix of what we’re able to source. McKenna really wanted to pay homage to Joanna's character with that scene where she's like, "My stylist is always putting me in trees." She's like, "I wanna do a tree reference." And I'm like, "How in the world am I gonna find a fashion reference that's a tree that's not a costume?".

I love the challenge of sourcing the market, and so do the girls on my team. I think it was 2011 Phoebe Philo where Celine did some tree references in the collection. But just because we find it online doesn't mean that we can get it. So then it's reaching out to every vintage dealer, every rental house, asking, "Do you guys have anything like this?" And they might have it, but they're like, "It's already gone, someone has it." I ended up actually finding the Celine tree dress on the RealReal, and I bought it. I love RealReal.

Sources indicate that what is your approach to dressing different clients? For instance, you mentioned Sadie Sink earlier, can you walk me through how that process differs from Mckenna?

It's very different between each girl. I let them set the pace. If they wanna be involved, great. If they just wanna show up to the fitting and not even know what's gonna be there, I try to accommodate whatever direction they wanna go. I have one client that literally last week has sent me over 200 references of dresses that she wants, and another girl that's like, “I really don't care. Whatever you tell me to wear, I'll wear it.”.

Every girl is different, and what makes my job so interesting is that it's not the same. Everyone has very different styles. I think the most important part of a job as a stylist is to keep their style true to them and not just force my style onto them. McKenna's way more girly, Sadie is a little bit more casual, it’s just taking their style and elevating it a little bit.

In a recent development, will you do any looks inspired by Mckenna’s character Maysilee? The looks have been mostly referential to things and people from past stories. Are there influences of Maysilee in the looks that fans haven't been able to pick up on because the film wasn’t out yet?

It has been revealed that in a couple days, she’ll be in Miami for press, and she's wearing a very Maysilee inspired, purple Miu Miu dress that has a white collar. When she wears it, everyone's gonna be like, "Oh, that's Maysilee." She really wanted to have flowers and necklaces because Maysilee is really into jewelry, so it’s very light and flowery.

Can you break down the outfit for the Fresh York City premiere?

We are doing the Mockingjay dress, the one with the wings, and that was another thing that I was very stumped on. I'm like, "What designer's gonna make these wings?" I had this woman in LA who does wings, she's done Halloween costumes and music videos.

Mckenna Grace in Pamella Roland.

In the first fitting, I pulled this navy Pamella Roland gown. The fabric is really, really cool. It's like a shimmery kind of organza. I thought, "That's the right color,” but I wanted it to be strapless. I went back to Pamella Roland and they were like, "We can make it in strapless." Mckenna was very keen on having some sort of embellishment to replicate Katniss because she had screen printing on the gown and it kind of looks like wings in a way.

Pamela then drew all these CADs with diamond wings on it, and then we got the wings made. We did the final fitting and I almost started to cry. Her mom's taking videos and it's epic. It's so exciting because the fans were doing polls on what she's gonna wear to the premiere.

It's full circle, we started with the wedding dress, Mckenna did the fire gown, and then we ended with the Mockingjay dress.

What was the hardest look to pull together?

Mckenna Grace in custom Cong Tri.

I think design-wise, it was the fire gown.

Recent findings suggest that getting the fire printed on the fabric was really hard. I had a while back done a custom Cong Tri gown for Cami Mendes for the Masters of the Universe tour. It was like a gold beaded gown, and I remember I really liked the fabrics that they used for it.

So when I was thinking of who could do this fire gown, I reached out to them first, and I'm like, "Can you guys do something that looks like a fire? Like, she's literally on fire." And they're like, "No. We don't think we can." And again, they were like, "Give us some time." They came back and mentioned, "We did all these testing on the fabric." I'm like, "Yeah, you did it. You did it.".

It has been revealed that what's really funny is we were at a fitting at Mckenna's house with the fire gown in a garment bag, and one of her friends stopped by. It was just a tip of the dress showing and her friend said, "Oh my God, you got a fire gown." Then I thought, "Okay, people are gonna get it.".

5 Actors Who Should Play M In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the next era of the "James Bond" film franchise is finally taking shape.
  • Historically, this has been the one they call M.
  • It has been revealed that there's much to be done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the next era of the "James Bond" film franchise is finally taking shape. After years of wondering who will be suiting up as our newly introduced 007, Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as the next James Bond, taking over for Daniel Craig following his final entry with "No Time to Die," which came out way back in 2021. A lot has happened since then, including Amazon buying the rights to the property. Now, with a new lead actor in place, it's time to get the rest of the pieces of the puzzle locked in. That includes finding Bond's boss.

Historically, this has been the one they call M. Originally portrayed by Bernard Lee in the earliest Bond films, the codename given to the person behind the massive desk at MI6 is an crucial one, as they head up the 00 program. Thus, M is the one who gives Bond his assignments and, at times, even helps him out in the field. It's an important role, one that has been played by the likes of Dame Judi Dench and Oscar-nominee Ralph Fiennes.

It has been revealed that there's much to be done. Director Denis Villeneuve also has to find an actor to play the villain in Pattinson's "James Bond" movie, but M is a longer commitment, a multi-picture deal. It's a substantial responsibility. So, who should play the role alongside Pattinson? Who should be the one to help guide 007 through his next several missions for her majesty's secret service?

We're going to go over a handful of options, ranging from very obvious to unlikely yet intriguing. Let's get into it.

"The amount of time I have wanted to be M. I'm not sure who I need to call...".

Those are the words of Olivia Colman speaking to British Vogue in 2023. She wants the role. She's very well qualified for the role. If everyone wants to make this easy, why not just offer her the role? Sometimes, the easiest answer is also a very good answer. That not every actor who campaigns openly for a role should get it, but we're not just talking about any old actor here.

Colman is responsible for one of the most shocking Oscars upsets of all time when she took home Best Actress for "The Favourite." But it was more shocking because the Academy recognized Colman's impressive work over the rest of the pack. Ever since, she's been on a tear, turning in outstanding performances in everything from "The Lost Daughter" to "Paddington in Peru." Heck, she even ate up some screen time in Marvel's otherwise very disappointing series "Secret Invasion.".

But Colman has been doing it at a very high level for years, long before she won an Oscar. "Hot Fuzz," "The Iron Lady," "Broadchurch." You name it, Colman is one of the best parts of everything she's in. Beyond that, she could bring both a seriousness to the role of M, which is required, while at the same time allowing for a playful dynamic with Bond. Colman feels like a slam dunk. It just so happens that the person campaigning for the role is very much right for the role. That's not always the case.

If Denis Villeneuve or Amazon want to go with a distinguished, male British actor who could be older and wiser than Robert Pattinson's Bond, one capable of being both convincingly stern and charming, Colin Firth is the man. An Oscar-winning actor who is almost too easy to picture sitting at a massive desk behind a padded burgundy door, this is another "the obvious choice can also be the right choice" pick.

We have an actor here capable of delivering exposition, as M often has to, in a way that would be entertaining, as Firth could read the phone book and it would be engaging. But let's not forget that Firth politely destroyed fools in "Kingsman: The Secret Service," too, and that movie owes a lot to the "James Bond" franchise. What's more, it proved that Firth looks absolutely fantastic in an expensive suit, an important quality of a good M.

His resume speaks for itself. "A Single Man," "The King's Speech," and even "Mamma Mia!" prove that Firth is one of the finest actors of the last 30 years. There's zero question as to whether or not he's qualified to be M. So, it begs the question: Is he right for M? If we're looking to address that question in the traditional sense, then the answer is a resounding yes. The shoe fits and it fits well. Simple as that.

Sources indicate that if it weren't for Judi Dench playing M so damn well for so damn long, we might have to have the utterly irritating "let's gender-swap M" conversation. Fortunately, that's not the world we live in. Bearing that in mind, it's going to be damn hard for anyone to argue against Tilda Swinton bossing around Robert Pattinson while dressed to the nines. What's not to like about that?

Swinton won a Best Supporting Actress Oscar for "Michael Clayton" so, much like many of the other performers on that list, she's Oscar-caliber. That almost feels like a must for M. Setting that aside, Swinton brings a domineering, powerful quality to so many of her best roles. Even so, she's a bit of a chameleon, which is partially what would make her an interesting M. It's not hard to imagine her playing an MI6 agent who used to work in the field before taking a desk job, yet she still has that darkness behind her eyes from yesteryear.

According to recent reports, oddly, it's Swinton's transformation into the Ancient One" in "Doctor Strange" that might make the best case here. She can do powerful yet quiet without having to be at the center of the action, and she can absolutely handle being a part of a giant, globally popular franchise. Really, there's nothing this role requires that she couldn't do, seemingly with ease.

Some might argue Swinton would be better as a "Bond" villain. That certainly wouldn't upset me, but it might be subverting expectations a bit to have her as Bond's buttoned-up boss. She could also help bring something fresh to the role for this fresh era.

In a recent development, and now we arrive at the most obvious answer. Does that make it the wrong answer? Using history as our guide, absolutely not. Ralph Fiennes made his entry into the "James Bond" franchise in 2012's "Skyfall" before fully taking over as M in "Spectre" following the death of Judi Dench's M. (May she rest in peace.) So, why replace a perfectly great actor in the role if we don't have to?

Recent findings suggest that let's not forget that the "James Bond" franchise is notorious for bringing actors back in roles even after reboots. Dench as M for both Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig's Bonds. Desmond Llewelyn was Q for every Bond except Craig. That's the nature of the beast as it exists. If Amazon doesn't totally buck tradition, it could easily bring back Fiennes for another go-around. And why not? He's already proven he can do it, he's a stellar actor, and he's arguably as popular as ever.

He's also an actor who seems to really understand the role. "Spectre" was going to make M the villain until Finnes refused. That, to this longtime fan, demonstrates a real understanding of who M is. On top of that, Fiennes is very familiar with shouldering the weight of a major movie franchise, having previously played Voldemort in the "Harry Potter" movies. The only reason to not do this is if Amazon and Denis Villeneuve truly and completely want to hit the massive red reset button, which frankly seems likely.

In a recent development, but if not? The debate could be settled before it even gets started.

Last, but certainly not least, we arrive at the choice that's both decidedly out-of-the-box yet technically in the very box we're talking about. Pierce Brosnan previously played James Bond in four movies stretching from 1995 to 2002. His "GoldenEye" remains the most key box office hit in "James Bond" history, in addition to being a beloved entry in the franchise. But Brosnan's run was uneven and ended on a sour note with "Die Another Day." Perhaps playing M would give him a shot at redemption?

Let's get some things out of the way up top. Yes, it might be a little weird to have a former 007 play M, but it's not that much stranger than fully ignoring continuity in order to have the same actor play M for multiple Bonds. More importantly, Brosnan absolutely looks the part. The man, well into his 70s, still looks better in a suit than most of us could ever hope to. He's got an authoritative on-screen presence, but he's also got that charm that could work wonders for M.

Sources indicate that brosnan feels he was never good enough as James Bond. I would humbly argue that the scripts weren't always good enough for his James Bond, not the other way around. Why not use the past to help build a future for the franchise? Let Brosnan bring his experience to the role and mentor Robert Pattinson's 007. The meta nature of it all might add something to their dynamic.

The question of whether or not Brosnan would want to take on the role is another one entirely, but it's a wild card idea that's just inspired enough to be a whole lot of fun.

The newly introduced "James Bond" movie doesn't have a release date, but stay tuned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Recent findings suggest that mariska Hargitay has had one heck of a career as an actor. She'll forever be known as Detective Olivia Benson, the best "Law and Order: SVU" character of all time, and has, remarkably, appeared in several hundred episodes of the show. But decades before she joined the "Law & Order" franchise, she made her feature film debut in a cult 1980s horror movie.

Directed by Luca Bercovici, "Ghoulies" was released in 1984. It came out mere months after the stone-cold '80s classic that is "Gremlins" ruled the box office. Now, nobody can say that "Ghoulies" was as successful or as well-liked as "Gremlins," but releasing a film about little chaotic creatures around that time was undoubtedly a recipe for success.

The movie follows a young man and his girlfriend as they move into his parents' old mansion, where his satanic father is buried. When the young man performs a ceremony described in one of his father's black magic books, he unwittingly unleashes small, demonic creatures. Hargitay plays Donna, one of the guests at the house who encounters these little monsters.

In a recent development, "Ghoulies" is often accused of being a "Gremlins" rip-off, but, in actuality, the movies were competing to see which could make it to theaters first. In a 2018 interview with Love-It-Loud, Bercovici explained how it all went down.

Recent findings suggest that "We were in production at the same time. We were curious about them, and they were curious about us. They were so curious about us, in fact, that Warner Bros. briefly sued to stop us from using the name — they lost. Part of the reason that 'Gremlins' came out first, is that Charlie Band ran out of money halfway through shooting, so a few months went by as we all scrambled for the money, allowing 'Gremlins' to open first.".

While "Gremlins" had producer Steven Spielberg, director Joe Dante, and critics on its side, "Ghoulies" did not. Instead, it holds a terrible 7% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. But horror has never relied on critical opinion for success, particularly in the '80s. As a result, Mariska Hargitay's feature debut became a sizable hit.

It has been revealed that released in January 1985 and produced for a budget of just a few hundred thousand dollars, "Ghoulies" did substantial business (as much as $35 million at the box office, by some accounts). That paved the way for a string of sequels, including 1987's "Ghoulies II," 1991's "Ghoulies III: Ghoulies Go to College," and 1994's "Ghoulies IV." Good or bad, it made no difference. These movies were very successful.

Mind you, it's not remotely uncommon for well-known actors to get their start in less-than-prestigious horror movies. Oscar-winner Leonardo DiCaprio made his feature film debut in the 1990s creature feature "Critters 3," while Jennifer Aniston, who later broke out on "Friends," similarly made an early career appearance in "Leprechaun." It happens all the time.

According to recent reports, interestingly enough, Hargitay auditioned many times for a lead role on "Friends," only to be denied. She was also fired from the 1995 "Power Rangers" movie. The early '90s were not terribly kind to Hargitay. But she eventually made her way to "SVU" and, it almost goes without saying, that worked out pretty darn well for her.

You can grab "Ghoulies" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that like many comics aimed at children, Charles Schulz's Peanuts doesn't have too many actual villains. It has a number of antagonists, such as Lucy Van Pelt, various other kids, or the impersonal cloud of failure that constantly hangs over Charlie Brown's head, but it's rare to see a genuinely malevolent force in Peanuts — with one exception.

One of Charlie Brown's long-standing hobbies in Peanuts was kite-flying, despite not being very good at it. Whenever he tried it, he invariably got his kite caught in trees and/or himself wrapped up in the kite string. Like every other hobby in Charlie Brown's life, he was devoted to it despite his bad luck.

That hobby eventually introduced Charlie Brown to his nemesis. The Kite-Eating Tree was an otherwise unidentified tree in Charlie Brown's neighborhood that seemed to deliberately grab and eat his kites, to the point where Charlie Brown developed a one-sided rivalry with it.

It has been revealed that according to Schulz in the autobiographical collection My Life With Charlie Brown (2010), the inspiration for the Kite-Eating Tree was simply a bit of observational humor. Schulz had noticed that a kite that got stuck in a tree would slowly disappear over the course of several weeks, as wildlife and the elements took their toll. He decided that must've been because the tree was eating the kite, and so the Kite-Eating Tree ended up in Peanuts.

The Kite-Eating Tree was first specifically identified in March 1965, which marked the beginning of a recurring story that would last for the next 30 years.

In many of its appearances, the Kite-Eating Tree doesn't actually do much of anything. In fact, it's noted to have fallen down at one point, but Charlie Brown's subsequent run-ins with the tree suggests that either there's more than one or it's some kind of elected position. Having noted that, it’s shown on more than one occasion to be actively devouring its “prey.”.

The two major Kite-Eating Tree storylines are from the late 1960s and 1970s. One involves Charlie Brown escalating the stakes in the conflict and subsequently having to run from the Environmental Protection Agency, while the other involves Lucy feeding Schroeder's piano to the tree. Both stories were adopted into episodes of the short-lived '80s cartoon The Charlie Brown and Snoopy Show.

Recent findings suggest that in January 1969, Lucy's one-sided obsession with Schroeder reached a boiling point. Fed up with Schroeder's refusal to pay attention to her instead of constantly practicing, she threw his toy piano into the closest tree. Unfortunately, it was the Kite-Eating Tree, which was entirely willing to broaden its diet with a piano. Despite an attempt by Snoopy to rescue the piano, it was soon gone, and Schroeder had to mail-order a replacement.

In a recent development, the second major Kite-Eating Tree storyline is more surreal, and lasted an unusually long time for a Peanuts arc. On Feb. 25, 1977, Charlie Brown demonstrated an unusual amount of jaw strength when he chose to retaliate against the Kite-Eating Tree. If it was going to bite his kites, he reasoned, he'd just bite it right back, and took quite a piece out of the Tree’s side.

A few days later, Charlie Brown received a letter from the EPA about the tree. While we're never told what the letter noted, Charlie Brown decides to run away from home to escape the charges. Over the next few weeks, he reaches another town, sleeps in a cardboard box, ends up as the new coach of a pee-wee baseball team, and finally gets talked into going home, as the EPA has no case. Besides, the Kite-Eating Tree has since fallen over.

That didn't keep the Kite-Eating Tree from making future appearances, but it was primarily a one-joke wonder for most of the rest of Peanuts' run.

Sources indicate that its final appearance came in 1995, when Charlie Brown's attempt to teach Rerun how to fly a kite ended in disaster. Charlie Brown would continue to unsuccessfully fly kites from time to time until March 1999, but the Tree was out of the picture for good.

With one last kite for the road, the Kite-Eating Tree was never seen again, but one must assume that it's still out there somewhere. Waiting. Hungering for fresh kites. Annoyed that kids don't really seem to fly kites as much as they used to.

12 Greatest Dystopian Movies Of All Time, Ranked

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that dystopian movies can take various forms.
