📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dystopian movies are a vast genre of cinema that will always be compelling, a means of exploring humanity's greatest fears about the future, the trajectory of oppressive government systems, and the collapse and reformation of entire societies. Countless dystopian movies have been made, from Blade Runner to The Hunger Games, though some are far more compelling and culturally significant than others.

Sources indicate that dystopian movies can take various forms. While plenty are gray, grim, and bleak, they can also be brighter animated family films, major action blockbusters, and/or huge spectacles that kick off entire franchises. Ultimately, all of them carry messages warning against the dangers of potential futures that are worse/more challenging than the present.

It has been revealed that the best and most memorable dystopian movies arguably balance entertaining storytelling and compelling concepts with unique world-building. Keeping that in mind, here's our ranking of the top 15 greatest dystopian movies/franchises of all time (from great to greatest, with honorable mentions including A Clockwork Orange, 28 Days Later, Gattaca, and RoboCop).

According to recent reports, michael Radford's adaptation of George Orwell's iconic novel Nineteen Eighty-Four remains a core foundation for so many dystopian movies that would come after. Set in a society controlled by "Significant Brother", free thought is considered dangerous, personal connections and relationships are forbidden, and the past is rewritten to serve the goals of the oppressive government. Exploring the concepts of invasive surveillance, propaganda, and overwhelming authoritarian control, the themes and warnings in 1984 are just as prevalent today, while still being one of the grimmest watches on this list.

The world of Bong Joon-ho's Snowpiercer involves a failed attempt to reverse global warming that has completely frozen the planet, leaving all of humanity's survivors on board a massive train that circles the Earth. Each car is divided by class, with the wealthy elite having the best accommodations while the less fortunate are in worse condition the further back you go. The movie stars Chris Evans as a leading revolutionary determined to make it to the front engine car and overthrow the ruling class.

An impressively direct and straightforward commentary on social inequality, the movie inspired a television series on TNT that ran from 2020-2024 (though the original movie was received much better). However, movies ranked higher on this list arguably have stronger nuance and more dimension to their core themes.

Industry observers note that steven Spielberg's Minority Report presents a future where nearly all murder in Washington, D.C. has been eliminated with a system known as PreCrime, using three precognitive psychics who predict crimes and make arrests before noted crimes are even committed. Starring Tom Cruise as a leading PreCrime officer who finds himself accused of a future murder, Minority Report is a fast-paced action thriller full of impressive futuristic set pieces and technology, featuring major themes and questions about free will, privacy, and what happens when too many individual rights are sacrificed in the name of security.

However, Minority Report's more singular focus on Tom Cruise's character and his personal goal of breaking the system means the world and its society are explored less than most would likely prefer.

Pixar's WALL-E takes place in a future where humanity has completely abandoned the planet and taken to the stars after covering the Earth with mountains of garbage and toxic waste, making the world uninhabitable. Living aboard a massive cosmic cruise ship while they wait for robots to clean up the planet, humans rely on technology for every aspect of their lives.

Despite being a family-friendly animated adventure starring the titular robot and his personal mission to find love with another robot named EVE, WALL-E still provides one of the greatest and most poignant environmental messages/warnings in all of cinema, as well as what humanity can lose the more we rely on technology in our lives. However, the movie does end on a hopeful note with Earth showing enough signs of growth and habitability for humans to return home. While WALL-E admittedly has a narrower scope of its dystopian society, its emotional storytelling and visual world-building make it one of Pixar's best films 18 years later.

According to recent reports, few science fiction franchises have built such an expansive dystopian world as the Planet of the Apes franchise. Beginning with Franklin J. Schaffner's 1968 original, the series imagines a future in which intelligent apes have replaced humanity as Earth's dominant species. When it comes to movie twists, few can beat the original film's iconic reveal that the planet was not an alien world, but, in fact, Earth itself in a dystopian future where humanity lost it all. Likewise, the franchise has continued for decades, with the most recent iteration of the franchise having produced some of the best dystopian movies in the modern era.

Two of the most notable entries include Dawn of the Planet of the Apes, when humanity is still struggling (and failing) to remain the dominant species, as well as the most recent Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes, which is set generations later. As such, the ability to explore so many different eras in the same world's complex dystopian timeline is a major advantage, even if some Planet of the Apes movies are more entertaining than others.

Set in a version of Great Britain ruled by an oppressive fascist government, V for Vendetta follows a young woman named Evey played by Natalie Portman, who finds herself involved with a masked revolutionary named V (Hugo Weaving). As V begins a one-man war against the entire corrupt government, Evey starts aiding V in his efforts as the film explores mass censorship, propaganda, and the enduring power and legacy of resistance amid its fairly straightforward messages about revolution. Featuring stylized visuals and impressive action, the movie is an easy rewatch every 5th of November.

It has been revealed that alfonso Cuarón's Children of Men (2006) imagines a truly bleak future where humanity has become infertile, leaving civilization on the brink of extinction, with Britain having gradually transformed into an authoritarian state. Rather than featuring some futuristic society with hi-tech visuals and the like, the movie is set in the year 2027 with an incredibly grounded approach as a former activist protects a woman who is remarkably pregnant, representing a massively rare source of hope for humanity's future it hasn't seen in years.

While it's certainly one of the bleakest films on this list, it's without a doubt one of the very best dystopian movies of all time (even if others are more memorable with greater cultural impact).

In a recent development, james Cameron's The Terminator franchise features one of the most popular dystopian futures and worlds in all of cinema. In the ashes of nuclear apocalypse, an AI system now known as Skynet takes over the world and wars with humanity, using machines and killer robots to hunt down the remaining human survivors. This includes going back in time and sending Terminators to the past to kill the mother of humanity's future savior before he can even be born.

It has been revealed that the franchise has since expanded into multiple films and shows, with many identifying Terminator 2: Judgment Day as the best entry overall. While the actual dark dystopian world of the future receives less screen time, it's the threat of this future and its efforts to rewrite the past that makes the franchise so compelling (that and killer robots ironically played by Arnold Schwarzenegger).

It has been revealed that based on Suzanne Collins' bestselling novels, The Hunger Games franchise takes place in Panem, a post-apocalyptic nation built on the ruins of what was once North America. Divided into 12 oppressed districts, with the wealthy elite living in the Capitol, yearly "games" are held, with children from each district being randomly selected to horrifically fight to the death to keep the population in line.

The first four movies focused on District 12's Katniss Everdeen, her survival after being chosen for the Hunger Games and her transformation into the major revolutionary known as "The Mockingjay" who helped topple the Capitol regime.

Industry observers note that however, the franchise continues to expand with dynamic prequels, continuing to flesh out the world of Panem, its history, politics, and key characters. This includes Sunrise of the Reaping, which has just been released in theaters and features a 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Combined with its predicted $120 million opening weekend, it feels pretty likely that The Hunger Games franchise will continue as one of the biggest and most culturally significant dystopian movie franchises of all time.

Recent findings suggest that without a doubt, The Wachowskis' Matrix franchise presents one of the most inventive and unique dystopian concepts in film history. Humanity has been unknowingly enslaved by intelligent machines, with their minds placed inside a simulated digital reality as their bodies are harvested for power. Keanu Reeves plays Neo, a computer hacker who discovers the truth and joins a rebellion against his artificial prison, while also becoming a messianic figure known as "The One.".

Sources indicate that exploring the nature of reality and our perceptions of what's real or not, free will, humanity's ever-growing technological dependence, faith, religion, and so much more all at the same time, the themes and ideas of The Matrix franchise are just as memorable as the groundbreaking action and visual effects that made the first movie and its sequels such definitive pillars of the dystopian genre. It's endlessly fascinating.

#85725. 58 Years Later, Captain Kirk's Best Star Trek Quote Is the Greatest Line in Sci-Fi History

58 Years Later, Captain Kirk's Best Star Trek Quote Is the Greatest Line in Sci-Fi History

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that some lines of dialogue become so famous they stop belonging to the movies and TV shows that produced them.
  • Recent findings suggest that star Trek: The Original Series has plenty of those.
  • But if I could only pick one line to represent everything Star Trek stands for, it would be four simple words spoken by Captain James T.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that some lines of dialogue become so famous they stop belonging to the movies and TV shows that produced them. “May the Force be with you.” “I’ll be back.” “You're gonna need a bigger boat.” You don't need to know the context. The words have long since transcended their original context and permeated the pop culture zeitgeist.

Recent findings suggest that star Trek: The Original Series has plenty of those. Spock’s wish that everyone to “Live long and prosper” is arguably the franchise's signature phrase. He also turned the simple word “fascinating” into a catchphrase simply by raising one eyebrow before saying it. Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley) spent three seasons reminding everyone, “I'm a doctor, not a…” and, at least in our collective memory declaring, “He's dead, Jim” while standing over the latest redshirt who wandered a little too far from the landing party.

But if I could only pick one line to represent everything Star Trek stands for, it would be four simple words spoken by Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) halfway through “Return to Tomorrow," the 20th episode of season 2:.

On the surface, it doesn't seem like an obvious choice. It's not printed on T-shirts nearly as often as “live long and prosper.” It isn't endlessly quoted by people who have never watched an episode of Star Trek. And unlike “beam me up, Scotty,” it never became part of the broader pop culture vocabulary. But that's exactly why it's the best quote. It doesn't just capture Kirk. It captures the entire philosophy of Star Trek.

First broadcast on Feb. 9, 1968, the episode “Return to Tomorrow” finds the Enterprise answering a mysterious distress call from a dead planet. There, Kirk and his crew discover Sargon, one of three survivors of an ancient civilization that has existed as beings of pure energy for half a million years. Sargon asks Kirk, Spock (Leonard Nimoy), and Dr. Ann Mulhall (Diana Muldaur) to temporarily surrender their bodies so he, his wife Thalassa, and the ambitious Henoch can build android bodies and begin life again. Dr. McCoy believes the aliens are manipulating them. Kirk believes the chance to learn from a civilization hundreds of thousands of years more advanced than humanity is worth the danger.

Sources indicate that the episode also marks the first of three Star Trek appearances by Diana Muldaur. She plays Dr. Ann Mulhall here before returning as Miranda Jones in the third season episode “Is There in Truth No Beauty?” Years later, she'd become a series regular on Star Trek: The Next Generation as Dr. Katherine Pulaski. “Return to Tomorrow” is also a fun piece of Trek trivia because it's one of the times Spock describes Sargon as “pure energy,” a phrase longtime fans immediately recognize.

Faced with allowing unimaginably powerful aliens to occupy the bodies of his crew, Kirk doesn't glitch an order. He makes an argument and reminds his crew that every leap forward in human history required someone willing to embrace uncertainty.

"They used to say if man could fly, he'd have wings," Kirk indicates. "But he did fly. He discovered he had to." He likens Sargon's offer to humanity's own journey from the Moon to Mars and eventually the stars, arguing that the potential for knowledge outweighs the danger. Only then does he arrive at the four words that define both the captain and the franchise. Those four words explain Kirk better than decades of pop-culture impressions ever could.

For years, pop culture has reduced Kirk to an oversimplified caricature: the swaggering captain who punches first, flirts with every alien woman he meets, and somehow loses his shirt during every other away mission. The real Kirk is far more thoughtful than that. He takes risks, certainly, but not because he enjoys gambling. He takes them because he believes some opportunities are too important to ignore.

Sources indicate that there's a world of difference between being reckless and accepting risk in pursuit of discovery. Kirk isn't arguing that danger is exciting. He's arguing that progress is impossible without it.

More importantly, he's explaining what separates Starfleet from almost every other organization. Plenty of fictional explorers travel because they're ordered to. Others do it for conquest, profit, or survival. Starfleet goes because knowledge itself is worth pursuing.

According to recent reports, that's why I think this quote is even more meaningful than the famous opening narration about boldly going where no one has gone before. The opening tells us what the Enterprise does. This one explains why.

The timing of the episode makes the speech even more remarkable. “Return to Tomorrow” aired in early 1968, roughly 17 months before Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. America was still trying to prove humans could successfully reach another world, and Star Trek was already imagining the next step beyond that. Kirk's speech places the Enterprise in the same lineage as every explorer who came before it, suggesting humanity's future won't be built by playing it safe.

According to recent reports, that idea has become the beating heart of Star Trek. Optimism, in the Star Trek universe, has never meant believing everything will work out. It means believing the unknown is worth facing anyway.

There are more famous quotes in The Original Series. There are funnier ones. There are certainly more quotable ones. But no other line distills what Star Trek has always been trying to say better than four words Kirk spoke nearly 60 years ago: “Risk is our business.”.

  • Guy Pearce plays Alexander Hartdegen, the inventor of the titular device, and he learns very quickly that mucking around with time travel doesn't always provide the result he's after.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that simon Wells' 2002 sci-fi flick "The Time Machine" was extrapolated from H.G. Wells' celebrated 1895 novel, one of the best sci-fi novels ever written, and also from George Pal's famed 1960 adaptation of the same story, itself one of the best time travel movies of all time. Made for a budget of $80 million, "The Time Machine" didn't overwhelm at the box office, earning almost $124 million worldwide. Critics were very unkind to "The Time Machine," and the film only has a 28% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 151 reviews.

The movie isn't great, reducing the intellectualism of Wells' original novel into a rote sci-fi action thriller, but there was a steampunk quirkiness to "The Time Machine" that could have been more openly embraced. It was even nominated for an Oscar for Best Makeup.

Guy Pearce plays Alexander Hartdegen, the inventor of the titular device, and he learns very quickly that mucking around with time travel doesn't always provide the result he's after. Alexander's motivation for building a time machine in the first place is to go back in time to prevent the murder of his fiancée (Sienna Guillory). This isn't part of the original novel, nor of George Pal's movie. Alexander spends five years building the time machine, and manages to save his fiancée, only to lose her again shortly thereafter. Something about the universe requires she die.

Sources indicate that this kicks off a long-ranging time-travel adventure wherein Alexander begins tripping through the centuries, hoping to find an answer about how fate operates. He eventually ends up in the very, very distant future — specifically, the year AD 802,701 — when humanity has evolved into two distinct subspecies, the Morlocks and the Eloi.

The two most notable additions to the movie of "The Time Machine" that most dramatically depart from the previous versions are characters played by Orlando Jones and Jeremy Irons. Jones' character is, I would argue, a good addition, adding someone for the protagonist to converse with. Irons' character is ... well, his inclusion is just baffling.

Jones plays Vox 114, an artificially intelligent digital library aide from the year 2030 who appears on glass screens. Because he is a computer, Vox is eager to teach people about science and the world. When Alexander, having just jaunted forward in time, asks Vox about time travel, Vox gets a little impatient, thinking Alexander just wants to talk about science fiction. Later in the film, Alexander finds Vox in a cave, somehow still operational hundreds of centuries later. Vox seems to have developed something of a consciousness over the years. He also still has a complete memory, remembering Alexander from this sojourn to 2030.

Recent findings suggest that irons, meanwhile, plays a character credited as the Über-Morlock, the psychic Cenobite-like leader of the Morlocks. As anyone who has read H.G. Wells' book can tell you, the Morlocks were an underground race of ape-like beings who feed on the Eloi who live on the Earth's surface. The Eloi, meanwhile, are placid, gentle, and defenseless. The idea is that the Morlocks evolved from old Earth's laboring classes, and the Eloi evolved from its aristocracy. Wells was clearly making a comment on class divisions, and how they will eventually play out if left to evolve along their logical extremes.

There is no Über-Morlock leading the underground monsters in the original book, and the inclusion of such a character in the 2002 movie is confusing and strange.

In a recent development, that said, there is at least something delicious about Jeremy Irons' performance. He sports a long white wig, pasty white skin, and wears a bizarre, black pleather outfit that looks like it could be worn to a bondage bar. "The Time Machine" climaxes with the Über-Morlock and Alexander grappling while the machine hurtles forward in time millions of years. It's such a kooky conceit that you might find yourself enjoying "The Time Machine.".

Sources indicate that some fun trivia: Simon Wells, the director of "The Time Machine" just happens to be the great-grandson of H.G. Wells. Simon Wells also co-directed the 1991 animated film "An American Tail: Fievel Goes West" (which was Jimmy Stewart's final film), as well as "We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story," the giant '90s animated hit "The Prince of Egypt," and several others. (He also helmed the massive Disney flop "Mars Needs Moms," but we'll forgive him this time.) All of this is to say that Wells was no neophyte in 2002, and he is not a traditional nepo baby who received an opportunity primarily because of his lineage.

Critics largely hated "The Time Machine." Roger Ebert gave the film one-and-a-half stars out of four, saying that it was "a witless recycling of the H.G. Wells story from 1895, with the absurdity intact but the wonderment missing." He noted that 800,000 years into the future, it was awfully convenient that Morlock and Eloi both seem to speak English. Guy Pearce's performance also didn't match the material. Ebert wrote that "Pearce, as the hero, makes the mistake of trying to give a good and realistic performance. Irons at least knows what kind of movie he's in, and hams it up accordingly.".

In a recent development, okay, so "The Time Machine" is not great. But Irons is fun. It certainly didn't deserve to bomb.

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Prequel film "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the details of how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada, Woody Harrelson in the original films) won the 50th Hunger Games ... and lost everything else in his life, turning him into a miserable man using alcohol to cope. Yet "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" revealed Haymitch wasn't merely the burnout he first appeared to be, but a key member of the rebellion against the Capitol.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the beginning of that, particularly Haymitch's early alliance with Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons, filling in for the late Philip Seymour Hoffman). Younger versions of several past Hunger Games victors first introduced in "Catching Fire" also show up in "Sunrise on the Reaping," including the tech wizard Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr. doing an uncanny vocal impression of original Beetee actor Jeffrey Wright).

In a recent development, beetee has already been caught rebelling against the Capitol. As punishment, his own son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV) was reaped into the Hunger Games. Beetee and Haymitch collaborate as part of a conspiracy to have Haymitch disrupt the arena's mechanical systems and, hopefully, sabotage the Games once he's inside. When Haymitch does so, but the Games persist and, when the conspiracy is discovered, he takes the fall. The Capitol has already done the worst thing it could to Beetee by taking his son, and as a victor, he's too valuable and visible a symbol to kill.

"Hunger Games" fans already know this isn't the last we've seen of Beetee, and this probably isn't the first you've seen of his actor who plays him. Born in Newly introduced Orleans in 1994, Harrison is the son of two musicians, but he chose acting as his primary creative path.

Harrison's film career began with incidental parts in "12 Years A Slave" and "Ender's Game" in 2013, which were followed by his first starring role in 2017's post-apocalyptic horror film "It Comes At Night." Harrison played the character of Travis, son of Paul (Joel Edgerton) and Sarah (Carmen Ejogo).

Recent findings suggest that in 2018, Harrison appeared in "Monster," Netflix's adaptation of Walter Dean Myers's 1999 novel about a Black honor student accused of murder. The following year, Harrison starred in a surprisingly similar film: the psychodrama "Luce," playing a former child soldier from Eritrea adopted by a wealthy white couple (Naomi Watts and Tim Roth). Luce is a straight-A student, popular athlete, and seemingly on his way to great things ... until he writes an essay that appears to defend radical political violence as a valid means of change.

Having proved himself with those leading roles, Harrison has continued making himself into one of Hollywood's most prolific young actors even before joining "The Hunger Games." Several of his prominent roles have been in historical dramas: In 2021, he played Black Panther leader Fred Hampton in 2021's "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and in 2022's "Elvis" he played Blues musician B.B. King. Harrison also played Martin Luther King Jr. in Season 4 of National Geographic series "Genius," opposite Aaron Pierre (now known as John Stewart from "Lanterns") as Malcolm X.

Recent findings suggest that but that's not all Harrison can do. He played Christian de Neuvillette in Joe Wright's 2021 musical film "Cyrano," adapting the 1897 French play by Edmond Rostand. In 2024 "Lion King" prequel "Mufasa," he voiced Scar. Being in organization with Jeremy Irons and Chiwetel Ejiofor is pretty impressive for an actor Harrison's age.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

Feel free to refer to the seven prompts listed below and try them out for yourself to see where your next book-filled adventures lead you next:.

And as an extra follow-up response, this next prompt can help ChatGPT do another round of evaluation to see which books truly match your tastes and weed out any made-up books it may have suggested:.

Now challenge your own recommendations. Which [number] books on this list are the weakest matches for my tastes, and why? Replace them with better alternatives. Don't invent titles or authors, and tell me where you're uncertain.

Industry observers note that running to ChatGPT to tell it to recommend you a bunch of upcoming and old books worth reading without being as descriptive as possible about your tastes is a waste of time. Netflix is experimenting with a latest approach to sitcoms as Minimum Wage prepares to return in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that while streaming platforms have become known for longer episodes, Netflix is experimenting with a shorter sitcom format. Now, one of the best newly introduced Netflix shows to binge is testing whether audiences are interested in episodes that run closer to 15 minutes.

In a recent development, according to Deadline, Minimum Wage is expected to return with 14 additional episodes in spring 2027, following its October debut. The workplace comedy, produced by Murder Mystery 2 director Jeremy Garelick and Will Phelps through American High, released its first 14 episodes with runtimes ranging from 12 to 20 minutes. However, it remains unclear whether the upcoming episodes will be considered the second part of season 1 or an entirely new season. Phelps explained why he believes shorter episodes could become a larger part of television's future:.

Recent findings suggest that "The future is these 15-minute kind of SpongeBob-length episodes where it’s really fast. There’s not any fat.".

Garelick also revealed that Netflix specifically requested shorter episodes when the streaming service acquired the series:.

It has been revealed that "When we closed the deal, [Netflix] remarked that they wanted it to be a minimum of twelve and a half-minute episodes. It was an interesting challenge because most episodic TV shows are 22 to 30 pages. It was almost like we were inventing a new structure as we were going and it was hard.".

The production team ultimately capped the episodes at 20 minutes, with shooting scripts running approximately 15 pages. The cast was also encouraged to improvise, combining traditional television writing with the fast-paced content designed for today's shorter attention spans.

According to recent reports, minimum Wage follows a group of teenagers working at The Slice Club, a pizza restaurant where everyday problems promptly become overwhelming. The comedy stars Grace Reiter, Aidan Micho, Hyde Healy, Julia Dicesare, Luke Burke, Ryan Micho, Tommy Armstrong, and WandaVision star Randall Park.

In a recent development, the approach builds on American High Shorts' established success on social media. According to Netflix, the production organization's sketches have accumulated over 7 billion views across platforms including YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat since launching in October 2022.

Before arriving on Netflix, Minimum Wage began as an American High Shorts series that accumulated over 30 million views across YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram since launching in May 2024. Following its October debut, the Netflix adaptation reached the streamer's global Top 10 with 2.4 million views, marking an early streaming achievement for the short-form comedy.

Sources indicate that other streaming comedies have also embraced shorter episodes. Netflix's Tires typically features episodes lasting around 20 to 23 minutes, while HBO Max's Stuart Fails to Save the Universe includes episodes as short as 15 minutes. Both series show how streaming comedies can vary in length without following a fixed episode runtime.

In a recent development, netflix initially ordered 20 episodes, but American High ultimately produced 28 after developing additional scripts. According to Garelick, the production team already has approximately 50 more draft scripts, leaving room for the comedy to continue beyond its upcoming release.

Minimum Wage is currently streaming on Netflix, with 14 additional episodes expected to arrive in spring 2027.

46 Years Later, the Most Influential Thriller of All Time Is Officially Free on YouTube

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that following the release of the genre-defining slasher Halloween, Cunningham and writer Victor Miller faced a real challenge: how to stand out in a subgenre flooded with horror movies (Black Christmas, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, to name just a few) trying to ride the slasher wave.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the years, corporations and filmmakers alike have eagerly sought to revisit the origins of horror classics (e.g., Bates Motel and Psycho, Welcome to Derry and IT, etc.) for modern audiences. It’s an easy way to find successwhen you already have an audience that loves the IP you’re reimagining.

Not even the Friday the 13th franchise has escaped the trend of revisiting the past. Crystal Lake, a latest series from A24 and Peacock, follows Pamela Voorhees (Betsy Palmer), Jason Voorhees’s deranged mother​​​​​​​. It’s a prequel that, frankly, nobody really asked for (though we kind of liked it anyway), since Jason’s origins have already been explored: Sean S. Cunningham’s 1980s horror film Friday the 13th — available to watch now for free on YouTube.

Sources indicate that following the release of the genre-defining slasher Halloween, Cunningham and writer Victor Miller faced a real challenge: how to stand out in a subgenre flooded with horror movies (Black Christmas, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, to name just a few) trying to ride the slasher wave. Friday the 13th had to be memorable, interesting, and stand out.

Sources indicate that on the surface, Friday the 13th doesn’t feel too different. It’s full of horny teens, heavy suspense, and a sense of isolation as a deranged killer hunts and kills them off, one by one. However, unlike other slashers like Halloween, Cunningham takes the brutality one step further by asking two very different but meaningful questions. Careful now, spoilers for a 46-year-old movie ahead.

It has been revealed that first, what if the killer were not a man in a mask but a vengeful mother driven mad by society’s disregard for her disabled son? Second, what if Cunningham and Paramount hired Tom Savini, famous for his work on George A. Romero’s Dawn of the Dead, to create some of the most gruesome deaths audiences had yet seen on the silver screen?

The result is one of the bloodiest slashers of all time, one that shook up perceptions of how grotesque the horror subgenre could be and who, exactly, could be the one dealing out those kills in the first place.

Slashers like Halloween and Black Christmas have some gnarly kills—who could forget Michael Myers pinning Bob to a pantry door with a large knife or Barb being stabbed with a unicorn figurine’s horn? Savini, however, elevated Friday the 13th’s kills into a bloody art form with shocking, realistic gore.

Recent findings suggest that savini did more than deliver, too. Just as he used practical effects for Dawn of the Dead, he did so again for several of the film’s kills. One especially memorable kill is counselor Jack’s, in which he’s stabbed in the neck as he lies in bed. Using a prosthetic neck piece and a pump, fake blood was pumped to create a blood-spurt effect that, for its time, looked remarkably realistic.

According to recent reports, the most significant thing that set Friday the 13th apart from its predecessors, however, was its killer: Pamela Voorhees. The slasher genre was no longer defined by masculine rage, but by a mother’s love. Even in the modern era of horror, slashers still feature far more male than female killers, but in 1980, Mrs. Voorhees was undoubtedly one of a kind.

Sources indicate that furthermore, for as deranged and murderous as she was, she exerted a strange, empathetic pull on audiences. Yes, murder is wrong — but you can’t deny that she loved her son. Unlike Michael Myers, who is often depicted as evil incarnate, Mrs. Voorhees has a complexity that made her brutal motives more compelling.

46 years later, Mrs. Voorhees's story begins anew with Crystal Lake. It’s unclear whether the series will get a second season, but even if it doesn’t, fans of Jason and his diabolical family tree needn’t worry. You can never go wrong with the original.

Friday the 13th is available to stream now for free on YouTube.

Industry News: Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived).
  • It has been revealed that “The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts.
  • It has been revealed that “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

It has been revealed that “The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

It has been revealed that “ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski stated. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

“You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski mentioned, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”.

According to recent reports, as Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

“I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”.

According to recent reports, one such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill mentioned. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”.

Industry observers note that “The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill mentioned, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were significant players.”.

Recent findings suggest that the substantial players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill mentioned of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”.

After Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill noted. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”.

Industry observers note that hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

It has been revealed that “I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill said. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”.

Sources indicate that hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill mentioned. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

In a recent development, “Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”.

Now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill mentioned, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you're the kind of person who has fun spotting celebrities in roles they took before they were launched to the heights of their fame, you could do a lot worse than throwing on a few episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and keeping your eye out for guest stars. Before he starred in "The Rocketeer" and took on the infamous Transylvanian count in "Bram Stoker's Dracula," Billy Campbell played the roguish Okona in "TNG's" second season, and before she had her breakout role in "Double Jeopardy" opposite Tommy Lee Jones, Ashley Judd made her acting debut in Season 5, playing an ensign in the episode where the crew of the Enterprise were all taken over by an evil video game.

In a recent development, these early appearances are always fun to catch, especially when the actor you're spotting is both immediately recognizable and just about to break out heights so high that you'd almost need a starship to catch up to them. The best example? Kirsten Dunst, who made an appearance in the final season of "The Next Generation," long before she'd star as Mary Jane Watson in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" films.

On the Season 7 episode "Dark Page", an 11-year-old Dunst played Hedril, a member of the Cairn, a species of alien telepaths who, as Captain Picard puts it, "have no concept of spoken language." To help facilitate communication, the Federation sends in their own telepath, occasional ambassador and perpetual thorn in Picard's side Lwaxana Troi (Majel Barrett), the mother of the Enterprise's empathic counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

Unfortunately, the Cairn's first attempt at connecting with an alien species goes awry, and Hedril winds up triggering Lwaxana's repressed memories of Deanna's older sister Kestra, who died when Deanna was a baby.

As a result, Dunst plays both Hedril and, in scenes where Deanna has to explore her mom's mindscape to find out while she's in a coma, a version of Kestra — who, it should be noted, had never been seen or mentioned before on the series, and was even unknown to Deanna.

The episode aired in 1993, and while it wasn't Dunst's first role as a child actress, it was the most prominent by far at the time. Of course, that would all change the following year with the release of "Interview With the Vampire," in which Dunst had her true breakout role playing the vampire Claudia, alongside Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt. Despite Pitt's difficulties in filming that led him to start feeling like an actual vampire, the movie was a financial and critical success, and Dunst in particular earned praise from Roger Ebert for the role and an MTV Movie Award for Best Supporting Actress and a Golden Globe nomination.

Dunst would go on to bigger fame as the star of the iconic cheerleading comedy "Bring It On" and, of course, the romantic lead of Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" trilogy. As for Hedril, she was one of many one-off characters who never returned to the Enterprise, but Kestra had a bit more of an interesting legacy. A novel set in an alternate universe called "Q and A" cast her, and not Deanna, as the counselor of the Enterprise, and in the first season of "Star Trek: Picard," it was revealed that Deanna would go on to name her own daughter Kestra in a tribute to her dearly departed sister.

#85716. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • Recent findings suggest that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

Industry observers note that the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

According to recent reports, for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

Recent findings suggest that while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

According to recent reports, the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

According to recent reports, this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

Industry observers note that if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

According to recent reports, to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

According to recent reports, [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.].

According to recent reports, at this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

Industry observers note that more concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In a recent development, in both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

Recent findings suggest that for her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

It has been revealed that but when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

Industry observers note that de Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

Industry observers note that when Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a fresh friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Industry observers note that josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

Recent findings suggest that this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

In a recent development, would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

Recent findings suggest that in the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

According to recent reports, here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand Newly introduced Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a big improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

Sources indicate that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.
